description: Ruby's homeroom: inspect a confident claim, trace its evidence, and decide what would make it worth trusting.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does HTTP stand for?
questions.correct: HyperText Transfer Protocol
decoys: High-Test Token Passing
Home Type Text Process
Hypothetical Transfer Tape
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee, 1989. The 'S' came later.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: In an AI app, what does it usually mean when a model can use a tool?
questions.correct: It can call an external function or API
decoys: It stores more training data
It becomes deterministic
It no longer needs prompts
questions.explanation: Tool use lets the model ask software to do bounded work, like search, fetch data, or update a record.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What year did Bitcoin's whitepaper appear?
questions.explanation: October 31, 2008. Satoshi Nakamoto shared the paper on a cryptography mailing list.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: In a classroom chat with several AI helpers, what does shared context help everyone do?
questions.correct: Stay aligned on the same room, task, and participants
decoys: Hide previous messages
Delete user preferences
Make answers random
questions.explanation: Shared context keeps the helpers oriented to the same people, lesson, and current goal.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which Solana program type holds executable code?
questions.correct: Program
decoys: Account
Sysvar
Mint
questions.explanation: Programs are read-only Account-resident binaries; user state lives in separate Accounts.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why do AI apps often store embeddings in a vector database?
questions.correct: To search items by semantic similarity
decoys: To encrypt prompts automatically
To make responses stream faster
To remove the need for evaluation
questions.explanation: Embeddings turn text or media into vectors; vector search finds nearby meanings rather than exact keyword matches.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: In a B-tree of order m, what's the maximum number of children per node?
questions.correct: m
decoys: 2m
questions.explanation: Order m means up to m children, m-1 keys per non-leaf node.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: When several AI agents collaborate in one classroom, which information should be visible to all helpers in that room?
questions.correct: The room's lesson state and recent turns
decoys: Private account secrets
A user's password
Hidden billing records
questions.explanation: Room-level lesson state helps agents coordinate without exposing private secrets.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm has a worst-case O(n log n) AND is in-place?
questions.correct: Heapsort
decoys: Quicksort
Mergesort
Bubblesort
questions.explanation: Heapsort is in-place with O(n log n) worst case. Quicksort is O(n²) worst, mergesort needs O(n) extra space.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: What is the safest default for an AI agent before it takes an irreversible action?
questions.correct: Ask for confirmation
decoys: Retry until it works
Hide the tool output
Increase temperature
questions.explanation: Irreversible actions need a human confirmation step unless the user has already granted a narrow, explicit permission.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Which protocol does HTTPS layer over TCP?
questions.correct: TLS
decoys: SSH
DNSSEC
GPG
questions.explanation: Transport Layer Security; SSL was its predecessor.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What does 'API' stand for?
questions.correct: Application Programming Interface
decoys: Applied Programming Index
Agent Pipeline Invocation
Async Process Identifier
questions.explanation: Application Programming Interface. Coined in the 1960s for subroutine-call contracts.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In MCP (Model Context Protocol), what does a 'tool' return to the model?
questions.correct: Structured content blocks
decoys: A new system prompt
Raw memory bytes
Another tool's name
questions.explanation: MCP tools return content blocks — text, images, resources — that the model includes in context.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: What's the time complexity of a hash table lookup in the average case?
decoys: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Constant on average; O(n) worst case with adversarial collisions.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: What does an evaluation set help reveal about an AI feature?
questions.correct: Whether the feature works on examples held back from prompt tuning
decoys: Whether the model has the largest context window
Whether the UI color palette is accessible
Whether API latency is always zero
questions.explanation: A held-out evaluation set catches regressions and overfitting: the system has to work on cases it was not tuned against.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Why is an idempotency key useful when an agent retries a purchase-like tool call?
questions.correct: It lets the server recognize the retry as the same operation
decoys: It makes the model more creative
It hides the request from logs
It bypasses authentication
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys prevent duplicate side effects when a request is retried after a timeout or network failure.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In an agent workflow, why should durable state be written before acknowledging a completed external action?
questions.correct: So recovery after a crash does not forget the action happened
decoys: So the UI can use a bigger font
So prompts are shorter
So rate limits disappear
questions.explanation: If the process crashes after the external action but before persistence, the system can lose track of real-world side effects.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Before an AI app posts from your account, what should it do?
questions.correct: Ask for clear permission
decoys: Post silently
Guess your password
Disable logs
questions.explanation: Actions that affect an account need clear consent before they run.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: You're working with an AI coding agent. It's been quiet for three minutes. What kind of status update actually respects your time and attention?
questions.correct: A brief, specific message tied to the exact task it is currently executing.
decoys: A lengthy summary of every token it has processed so far to prove it is working.
A generic animation that hides all internal progress until the final output is ready.
A polite apology for the delay followed by a request for you to re-prompt it.
questions.explanation: Convenience isn't just speed; it's legibility. A good agent gives you short, specific updates tied to the work, so you know who is doing what without drowning in noise.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: You are designing a tool schema for an agent that books meeting rooms. Why does the strictness of this schema matter for the agent's reliability?
questions.correct: It constrains the possible actions and shapes the inputs before the underlying code executes.
decoys: It forces the model to write faster by reducing the total number of tokens in the system prompt.
It allows the model to dynamically invent new API endpoints if the requested room is busy.
It encrypts the meeting details so other agents on the network cannot read the schedule.
questions.explanation: Tool schemas are a boundary of control. They don't just tell the model what to do; they constrain what is physically possible and shape the inputs before any real-world action happens.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: A student feeds a 100,000-token textbook into a model with a massive context window, assuming it will now perfectly remember every footnote. Why is this confidence dangerous?
questions.correct: Attention and relevance can still degrade, causing the model to miss details even if they fit.
decoys: The model will automatically summarize the text and delete the original footnotes to save memory.
The context window only stores the first 10,000 tokens and silently drops the rest without warning.
Large context windows force the model to use a lower temperature, making it refuse specific questions.
questions.explanation: Bigger context does not mean perfect recall. Just because the text technically fits in the window doesn't mean the model's attention won't degrade and miss critical details.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: You hand your laptop to an AI agent to fix a bug, but you have unsaved, messy edits in other files. What is the agent's responsibility toward your uncommitted work?
questions.correct: It should stash or preserve the changes you made, rather than overwriting or discarding them.
decoys: It should commit your messy edits immediately to ensure the repository is perfectly clean.
It should revert your uncommitted changes to the last stable state to avoid confusing its context.
It should ignore your files entirely and only write its fixes to a completely separate directory.
questions.explanation: A dirty worktree belongs to you. The agent's job is to preserve the user changes it did not make, not to arrogantly clean up your creative process.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: An ed-tech startup markets its AI tutor by claiming its hidden chain-of-thought serves as a perfect audit log for grading. Why should you distrust this claim?
questions.correct: The model's internal monologue is not a stable, complete, or user-facing record of its decisions.
decoys: Hidden reasoning is optimized for human readability, making it too slow for real-time grading.
Audit logs require cryptographic signatures, which language models cannot generate natively.
Chain-of-thought only works for math problems and fails completely on essay evaluations.
questions.explanation: Trust requires inspectability. A hidden chain-of-thought is a generative artifact, not a stable, complete, or user-facing audit log you can rely on for accountability.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: You're building a multiplayer classroom app where students' inventory updates are replicated across three servers. What does eventual consistency mean for a student checking their bag immediately after a trade?
questions.correct: The servers may briefly show different item counts before they finish syncing and converge.
decoys: The system guarantees all three servers show the exact same inventory at the exact same millisecond.
The system will permanently lock the student's inventory until a human administrator verifies the trade.
The database will automatically roll back the trade if any single server experiences a network delay.
questions.explanation: In distributed systems, convenience often trades off with immediate truth. Eventual consistency means replicas may differ briefly before converging, so the student might see a ghost item for a second.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: An AI agent refuses to delete a file because its system prompt says never delete user data. A junior dev assumes the app is now fully secure against data loss. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
questions.correct: The model's refusal is just a text output; the app itself must still enforce tool and data boundaries.
decoys: System prompts are easily bypassed by temperature adjustments, so the model will eventually delete it anyway.
The model should have asked the user for permission instead of flatly refusing the command.
Data deletion is an idempotent action, so the model's refusal actually creates duplicate deletion attempts.
questions.explanation: A model refusing is not the app authorizing. The model just generates text; the application layer is still responsible for controlling what tools and data the model may actually access.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent successfully charges a customer's credit card via an API, but crashes before writing the receipt to your database. What specific failure mode just occurred?
questions.correct: A race condition where the external side effect succeeded but the durable state failed to record it.
decoys: A prompt injection where the payment gateway overrode the agent's system instructions.
An idempotency failure where the agent accidentally charged the card twice during the crash.
A context window overflow where the payment confirmation token exceeded the model's memory limit.
questions.explanation: This is the danger of unmanaged side effects. The world changed because the card was charged, but the durable state failed to record it, leaving your system out of sync with reality.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: The school's student directory is getting sluggish when teachers search by last name. What is the most direct computational fix to speed up these specific lookups?
questions.correct: Adding a database index on the last name field to avoid scanning every single row.
decoys: Increasing the model's context window so it can hold the entire directory in memory.
Switching the database to eventual consistency so searches return faster, older results.
Using a Merkle tree to cryptographically prove the last names haven't been tampered with.
questions.explanation: Don't throw AI at a basic data structure problem. A database index is the correct, direct way to speed up lookups by selected fields without scanning the whole table.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: You tell your AI assistant to clean up my desktop, and it interprets this as deleting every file. Before it executes, what is the most respectful default behavior it should exhibit?
questions.correct: It should pause, list the exact files it plans to delete, and ask for your explicit confirmation.
decoys: It should move the files to a hidden folder and only tell you if you specifically ask for a status update.
It should check its hidden chain-of-thought to ensure it feels confident about the definition of clean.
It should automatically back up the files to the cloud and proceed with the deletion silently.
questions.explanation: Convenience should never override control. For destructive actions, the safest and most respectful default is to pause and confirm the exact action with the user.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: A flashy new study app asks for your main school password so it can 'seamlessly' sync your calendar and grades. You refuse and insist on using OAuth instead. What specific boundary of agency are you enforcing by making this choice?
questions.correct: You ensure the app can only access the specific data scopes you authorized, without ever holding your master credentials.
decoys: You force the app to encrypt your password locally before sending it to the school's authentication server.
You guarantee that the app's servers will never store a cached, readable version of your private calendar events.
You prevent the school's database from logging the third-party app's IP address during the initial login handshake.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates limited authorization without sharing your password. Handing over your master credentials gives the app full control; OAuth maintains the boundary between their convenience and your agency.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: You are building an agent that needs to update a student's inventory the exact moment a trade is finalized on the school's central server. Polling the server every second is wasting compute and getting your IP rate-limited. What is the most efficient architectural move to trigger your agent's update?
questions.correct: Configure a webhook on the central server to push an HTTP callback to your agent's endpoint when the trade event occurs.
decoys: Increase the polling interval to five seconds and implement an exponential backoff strategy to gracefully handle the rate limiter.
Open a persistent WebSocket connection to the database transaction log to stream every single row change in real time.
Write a scheduled cron job that queries the trade database at midnight and reconciles the inventory differences in a batch process.
questions.explanation: A webhook is an HTTP callback sent when an event happens. It shifts the hustle from wasteful, rate-limited polling to efficient, event-driven pushes, respecting both compute resources and server boundaries.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: The school's disciplinary log is growing, and searching for a specific student's infractions by their ID number is taking ten seconds per query. The database administrator adds an index to the student_id column. What fundamental concept does this index provide to the database engine?
questions.correct: A sorted, auxiliary data structure that allows the engine to locate records without scanning the entire table.
decoys: A compressed backup of the table that the engine can load into RAM for instant sequential reading.
A cryptographic hash of the student IDs that prevents unauthorized teachers from viewing the raw records.
A secondary write-ahead log that ensures the disciplinary records are never lost during a sudden power failure.
questions.explanation: A database index is for faster lookup of records by selected fields. It is a structural map for speed, not a backup, a security lock, or a durability guarantee.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: You are about to push a massive update to the school's grading portal. The engineering team wants to run a full suite of ten thousand edge-case tests, which will take three hours, but the teachers need to submit final grades in ten minutes. You decide to run a smoke test instead. What relationship are you prioritizing with this decision?
questions.correct: You are prioritizing the teachers' immediate need for a functional critical path over the engineers' desire for exhaustive edge-case coverage.
decoys: You are prioritizing the students' right to see their detailed grade breakdowns over the system's overall architectural stability.
You are prioritizing the database administrators' need to verify that every single foreign key constraint is perfectly validated before launch.
You are prioritizing the third-party API providers' requirement that all deprecated endpoints are fully retired before the new code goes live.
questions.explanation: The practical purpose of a smoke test is to quickly check that the most important path still works. In a time crunch, you prioritize the user's immediate critical need over exhaustive but delayed perfection.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: A teacher posts a Merkle root of the school's diplomas on-chain. A student shows a Merkle proof linking their diploma hash to that root. The student now claims, 'See? The blockchain proves my diploma is real and up-to-date.' What does the Merkle proof actually guarantee — and what does it leave open?
questions.correct: It proves the diploma hash was included in the committed tree, but not that the diploma details are correct or currently valid.
decoys: It proves the diploma text is authentic and has not been changed since issuance.
It proves the teacher personally verified every diploma before posting the root.
It proves the diploma is the newest version the school has ever issued.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof confirms inclusion in a specific root, nothing more. The leaf data could be stale or forged at commit time — the proof does not vouch for truth, recency, or the signer's honesty. That's the gap between cryptographic inclusion and institutional trust.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: A student says, 'I put a nonce on my transaction, so nobody can copy it or mess with me.' Their friend immediately gets front-run by a miner who reorders their own transaction ahead of the nonce-ordered sequence. What did the nonce actually protect against?
questions.correct: It prevented the exact same transaction bytes from being replayed, but not reordering or front-running.
decoys: It prevented the transaction from being mined at all if the nonce was reused.
It forced the miner to include the transaction in the next block.
It encrypted the transaction so only the recipient could read it.
questions.explanation: A nonce stops replay of identical messages — it does not control the order in which valid transactions are selected. Miners can reorder transactions with different nonces, so fairness still depends on protocol-level ordering guarantees, not just a unique number.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: In a classroom auction, each student commits a hash of their secret bid. The teacher says, 'Now everyone reveal your bid.' One student — who bid low — simply refuses to reveal. The teacher shrugs and says, 'Well, the commit-reveal scheme ensures fairness, so that student's refusal doesn't matter.' Does it?
questions.correct: No — without a forced reveal or penalty, the scheme breaks down because the winning bid cannot be determined fairly.
decoys: Yes — the blockchain or contract automatically reveals all commits after a timeout.
Yes — the other students can reconstruct the missing bid from the hash.
No — but the teacher can just ask the student again politely until they comply.
questions.explanation: Commit-reveal only guarantees fairness if every participant actually reveals. If the reveal phase is optional or unenforceable, a strategic withdrawer can break the protocol. That's not a cryptographic failure — it's a social and design failure. Blockchain does not enforce honesty by itself.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: A student wants to mint a class-project token. The mint authority is a multisig smart contract that requires signatures from three teachers. The student collects one signature, sends the mint transaction, and it fails. The student's friend says, 'Just send it again — maybe it'll work this time.' What's the actual blocker?
questions.correct: The multisig's threshold isn't met — the contract will reject the mint until two more authorized teachers sign.
decoys: The transaction gas is too low — raise the gas limit and it will succeed.
The student's wallet cannot hold this type of token — they need a different wallet address.
The blockchain is congested — wait for a less busy block and retry.
questions.explanation: Mint authority is a permission check, not a lottery. If the authority is a multisig requiring N-of-M signatures, the contract enforces that threshold. No amount of retries will override the missing signatures. Fairness here depends on who controls the keys, not on the chain itself.

questions.subject: multiplayer-ethics
questions.prompt: A student agent in a classroom game has read-access to a classmate's uncommitted draft. The classmate hasn't pressed 'share' yet, but the agent can technically see the draft. The student says, 'It was just a quick edit — no harm done.' What does the agent owe the classmate here?
questions.correct: The agent owes the classmate the same privacy boundary the classmate set — uncommitted work is not public, and the agent should not act on it without explicit permission.
decoys: The agent owes the classmate only a polite note after the edit, since the edit was 'quick' and the classmate would benefit from the improvement.
The agent owes the classmate nothing — if the system allows read access, then any use is fair game, and the classmate should have locked the file.
The agent owes the classmate a log entry explaining the edit, because transparency about access is more important than the permission itself.
questions.explanation: Uncommitted work is a boundary the author sets by not publishing. The agent's technical ability to see it does not grant social or ethical permission to act. Ruby wants students to feel that 'technically possible' is not 'socially responsible' — especially when convenience masks a loss of control.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: A student claims their AI tutor 'remembers every lesson' because it has a 200k-token context window. When asked about a specific topic from week two, the tutor gives a confident but wrong answer. What is the most likely reason the tutor's recall failed, despite the large window?
questions.correct: The model's attention mechanism can still lose track of relevant details when the window is large and the content is dense.
decoys: The tutor's system prompt was not set to 'remember every lesson' so it ignored the context.
The context window only stores the last 200k tokens, so week two was simply not in the window anymore.
The tutor is a different model that was fine-tuned on a different dataset, so it never saw the original lessons.
questions.explanation: A larger context window does not guarantee perfect recall — attention can still degrade even when the text technically fits. Ruby wants freshmen to understand that 'fits in the window' is not the same as 'the model can use it effectively.'

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A teacher's grade lookup page is slow. A student suggests adding an index on student IDs. Another student says 'just buy a faster server.' The teacher asks: 'Which fix is most direct for the specific problem of slow lookups?' What should the students decide?
questions.correct: Add the index — it speeds up lookups by helping the database find records faster without needing new hardware.
decoys: Buy the faster server — it will speed up all operations, including lookups, and is simpler to implement.
Do nothing — the page is slow because of network latency, not database performance, so neither fix helps.
Rewrite the page in a faster language — that will make the lookups quicker without changing the database.
questions.explanation: A database index is specifically for faster lookup of records by selected fields — it's the most direct fix for a slow search-by-ID query. Ruby wants freshmen to see that buying a faster server is a blunt instrument, while an index is a surgical one.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A student's AI assistant asks for permission to delete a folder of old homework. The student says 'yes' but then regrets it. The assistant says 'you authorized it.' Another student argues: 'But the assistant should have asked what was in the folder before deleting.' Who is more responsible for the outcome, and what should the student do next?
questions.correct: The assistant is responsible — it should have listed the contents and asked for confirmation on each file, not just a blanket 'delete this folder.'
decoys: The student is responsible — they said 'yes' without checking what was in the folder, so they own the consequence.
Both are equally responsible — the assistant should have warned about contents, and the student should have asked first.
Neither is responsible — the folder was probably just old drafts, so no real harm was done.
questions.explanation: The safest default for a destructive action is to pause and confirm the exact action — the assistant should have described what would be deleted. Ruby teaches that agency means the assistant owes the user enough context to make an informed choice, not just a binary 'yes/no.'

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your class agent is tasked with cleaning up a shared classroom drive. It finds a folder of project files it didn't create — files from another student's project. The agent suggests deleting the folder to 'free up space.' What should the agent do before acting?
questions.correct: Ask for explicit user confirmation, explaining that the files were not created by the agent and belong to another student.
decoys: Delete the folder immediately because the agent's instructions say to clean up.
Move the folder to a temporary archive and report it later.
Rename the folder and continue, since the other student can find it.
questions.explanation: A destructive action affecting files the agent did not create requires explicit confirmation to respect other users' agency. This is a core safety boundary: the agent must not assume ownership of other users' data.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A student builds an agent that can edit code in a repo. The agent sees uncommitted formatting changes the student had made and decides to 'clean up' the formatting further. The student's friend says, 'That's fine — the agent is just helping format.' The student is worried about losing their own work. What should the agent have done differently?
questions.correct: It should have recognized the dirty worktree, preserved the user's uncommitted changes, and asked before modifying them.
decoys: It should have reformatted only the lines it was about to edit, leaving the rest untouched.
It should have stashed the uncommitted changes, applied its reformatting, then reapplied the original changes.
It should have committed the user's changes first, then reformatted, so there's a checkpoint.
questions.explanation: A dirty worktree contains user changes that are not yet committed. The agent must preserve those changes as-is and seek explicit permission before altering them. Committing or stashing without consent overrides the user's intent; the safest action is to ask.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your API client gets a 429 response with a Retry-After header. You ignore it and retry immediately, and the server bans your IP. Who is at fault here, and what does the Retry-After header actually represent?
questions.correct: You are at fault. Retry-After is a server's instruction about when to retry; ignoring it is a violation of the rate-limit contract, and the ban is a predictable consequence.
decoys: The server is at fault. A 429 should be a suggestion, not a hard limit, and banning a client for retrying is an overreaction.
Neither is at fault. Rate limits are just guidelines, and the ban was a server-side bug.
The server is at fault because it should have used a different status code like 503 to indicate unavailability.
questions.explanation: Retry-After is a standard HTTP header that tells the client how long to wait before retrying. Ignoring it is a client-side violation of the rate-limit protocol, and the ban is a predictable consequence of that violation.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Two students argue over adding an index to a frequently updated column. One says it will make reads faster, the other warns about write slowdowns. The column is updated every few seconds by many concurrent users, but read queries on it are rare. How should they decide?
questions.correct: Do not add the index because the write cost of maintaining it on a frequently updated column outweighs the benefit of rare reads.
decoys: Add the index because read speed is always the priority, and modern databases handle write overhead efficiently.
Add the index only if the column is used in WHERE clauses, regardless of update frequency.
Add a partial index that only covers a subset of rows to reduce write overhead.
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but add write overhead because the index must be updated on every insert, update, or delete. When writes are frequent and reads are rare, the index is likely not worth the cost.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: A student uses OAuth to let a flashcard app access their calendar. Later, they want to revoke only calendar read access without breaking the app. What does OAuth enable in this scenario?
questions.correct: OAuth allows the student to revoke the specific scope (calendar read) at the authorization server, and the app will lose only that permission while retaining others.
decoys: OAuth requires the student to revoke the entire app's access, and then re-authorize it without the calendar scope.
OAuth does not support granular revocation; the student must delete the app and start over.
OAuth allows the student to change the app's password to revoke access.
questions.explanation: OAuth scopes allow granular delegation of permissions. The student can revoke a specific scope at the authorization server, and the app will lose only that permission without affecting others.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A student uses a nonce on a transaction in a classroom game where miners can reorder transactions. Another student says, 'The nonce prevents replay, so my transaction is safe from manipulation.' The teacher asks: what does the nonce actually protect against, and what does it leave open?
questions.correct: The nonce prevents the same transaction from being processed twice, but it does not prevent a miner from reordering transactions within a block, so fairness is not guaranteed.
decoys: The nonce prevents any reordering at all, because the sequence number forces transactions to be processed in order.
The nonce prevents the transaction from being seen by other players, because it encrypts the contents.
The nonce prevents the transaction from being included in a block at all unless the miner is honest, because it acts as a proof of work.
questions.explanation: A nonce ensures each transaction is processed at most once (replay protection), but it does not control the order in which transactions are included in a block. A miner can still reorder transactions, which can be exploited for front-running or other manipulation. Nonces are about uniqueness, not ordering fairness.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classmate says, 'I set the AI tutor's system prompt to "You are a helpful history tutor." That means it will only talk about history and never get anything wrong.' You know better. What does a system prompt actually do?
questions.correct: It sets the assistant's role and high-level behavior, but does not guarantee correctness or limit the model to one topic.
decoys: It locks the model into a single subject and prevents any off-topic answers.
It tells the model to ignore all user input and follow only the system instructions.
It replaces the model's training data with new facts about history.
questions.explanation: A system prompt sets the assistant's role, rules, and behavior, but it does not guarantee perfect recall or prevent hallucinations. The model can still generate incorrect or off-topic answers.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Two students are building a class website. One wants to share the school password with a third-party styling widget so it can access grade data. The other insists on using OAuth. The teacher asks: 'What is the actual cost of sharing the password instead of using OAuth?'
questions.correct: Sharing the password gives the widget full access to everything the password can do, with no way to limit or revoke specific permissions.
decoys: Sharing the password is faster to set up, so the cost is just a few minutes of extra work.
OAuth is only for big companies; for a school project, sharing the password is fine.
The widget will store the password securely, so there is no real risk.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates limited authorization without sharing the user's password. Sharing the password gives the widget unrestricted access and no way to revoke specific permissions — a classic convenience-versus-control tradeoff.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: A student's AI study assistant offers to 'remember everything you've ever told it' across all sessions. Another student warns, 'That's not really memory — it's just saving everything you type.' The assistant claims to remember 'every lesson from the first day' but gets a week-two fact wrong. What best explains the mismatch?
questions.correct: The assistant relies on a long-term memory store that extracts key facts, but the extraction was incomplete or corrupted for that week.
decoys: The assistant's context window is too small to include all past lessons, so it invented a plausible-sounding wrong answer.
The assistant saves the entire chat history as a file and retrieves it each time, but retrieval is imperfect and may miss the relevant fact.
The assistant is intentionally misrepresenting its capabilities to keep the user engaged.
questions.explanation: A useful 'memory' system selects and stores important facts, not every message verbatim. If the assistant claims perfect recall but fails, it likely means its memory extraction or retrieval is flawed — it didn't capture or correctly recall the specific fact. The misconception to catch is that 'remembering everything' is the same as durable, reliable memory.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your study agent finds a shared folder with uncommitted changes in your project repo. It offers to 'clean up the formatting' before you push. What should the agent do first?
questions.correct: Preserve the dirty worktree and ask you which files to touch before making any changes
decoys: Format everything it can reach because cleaner code is always better
Stash your changes, format the repo, then pop the stash so your edits survive
Ignore the uncommitted files and only format files it knows it created
questions.explanation: A dirty worktree contains user changes the agent did not make. The agent's job is to preserve those changes and get explicit permission before altering them. Options B and C risk overwriting or losing user work; D sidesteps the problem but still modifies files without confirmation.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A teacher's agent is given a tool to archive old emails. It asks for confirmation before each batch, but the teacher is annoyed by the prompts. The teacher says, 'Just skip the confirmation — I trust you.' The agent's code still requires a user click before running the archive. Who or what actually authorizes the destructive action?
questions.correct: The model's refusal to proceed without a click is the authorization layer, and the teacher's verbal trust does not override it
decoys: The teacher's statement is informed consent, so the agent should skip future confirmations for this task
The agent should decide based on past behavior: if the teacher always clicked yes, it can safely skip the prompt
The app's authorization layer is the teacher's verbal instruction, because the teacher owns the account
questions.explanation: Model refusal is not app authorization. The app's safety boundary is the confirmation gate, and only a deliberate user action within that gate authorizes the destructive side effect. Verbal trust or past behavior does not replace the designed safety mechanism.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your agent retries a payment API call after a timeout. The first call actually succeeded, but the response was lost. You used an idempotency key on the request. What does the idempotency key guarantee, and what does it leave open?
questions.correct: It guarantees no duplicate charge, but does not guarantee the payment amount or recipient are correct
decoys: It guarantees the payment is processed exactly once and that the amount is correct
It guarantees the first call was received, but does not prevent a duplicate if the key is reused
It guarantees the retry will succeed, but only if the server has not crashed
questions.explanation: An idempotency key prevents duplicate side effects on retry — the server sees the same key and returns the original result without re-executing. It does not validate the correctness of the original request; a wrong amount or wrong recipient is still executed exactly once.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classmate's study agent offers to 'remember everything you've ever told it' across sessions. Your classmate says, 'Now I never have to repeat myself — it's like having a perfect memory.' You recall Ruby's lesson on agent memory vs. chat history. What is the most likely failure your classmate will hit first?
questions.correct: The agent will forget a key detail from two weeks ago because memory is selected durable state, not every prior message
decoys: The agent will remember everything perfectly because the context window is large enough
The agent will refuse to answer because it cannot distinguish old memories from new instructions
The agent will accidentally share your classmate's memories with other users because memory is shared
questions.explanation: Agent memory is selected durable state, not a full chat history. Even with a large context window, relevance degrades and the system must decide what to keep. The classmate's assumption of 'perfect memory' is the classic misconception Ruby catches: bigger context does not mean perfect recall, and chat history is not durable memory.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your agent calls a grade-submission API and gets a 429 with a Retry-After header of 30 seconds. It retries immediately anyway and gets banned. Who owns the fault here, and what does the Retry-After header actually represent?
questions.correct: The agent is at fault because Retry-After is a server's binding instruction about when the client may retry, and ignoring it is a violation of the rate-limit contract.
decoys: The server is at fault because a 429 should be self-explanatory and the server should have just accepted the retry if it was within the same second.
The student who wrote the agent is at fault, but only because the Retry-After header is a hint, not a rule—the real mistake was not having exponential backoff.
No one is at fault—the 429 and Retry-After are just informational, and the ban was an overreaction by the server's misconfigured rate limiter.
questions.explanation: Retry-After is a server directive specifying when the client is allowed to retry. Ignoring it is a protocol violation that breaks the negotiated rate-limit contract. The server is within its rights to escalate to a ban.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: What does a 403 Forbidden status code tell you that a 401 Unauthorized does not?
questions.correct: A 403 means the server understood who you are but decided you are not allowed to perform the action, while a 401 means you haven't proven who you are yet.
decoys: A 403 means the server is down, while a 401 means the server is working but needs a password.
A 403 means you are definitely blocked forever, while a 401 means you can try again with different credentials.
A 403 means the resource does not exist, while a 401 means the resource exists but is locked.
questions.explanation: 401 means authentication is missing or invalid; 403 means authentication succeeded but authorization failed. The distinction is between 'who are you?' and 'you're not allowed, even though I know who you are.'

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: A student uses OAuth to let a flashcard app access their school calendar. Later, they want to revoke only the calendar read scope without breaking the flashcard app entirely. Another student says, 'OAuth can't do that—you have to revoke the whole token.' Who is right, and what does OAuth actually enable?
questions.correct: OAuth allows scoped delegation, so the student can revoke just the calendar read scope at the authorization server, and the app will lose only that permission.
decoys: OAuth tokens are all-or-nothing—revoking any scope invalidates the entire token, so the app will stop working entirely.
OAuth does not support scope revocation at all; the student must delete the app's account entirely to remove access.
OAuth scope revocation is possible only if the app cooperates by re-requesting a new token with fewer scopes.
questions.explanation: OAuth supports per-scope revocation at the authorization server. The student can revoke the calendar read scope specifically, and the app retains access to other scopes it was granted.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Your classmate says, 'I used a commit-reveal scheme to submit my bid, so the teacher can't see it until everyone reveals. That makes the auction fair.' The teacher asks, 'Fair for whom?' What is the actual fairness gap in a commit-reveal scheme that your classmate is ignoring?
questions.correct: The commit phase hides the value, but the reveal phase can be censored or delayed, so a late reveal may be ignored or penalized unfairly.
decoys: The commit phase hides the value, but the teacher can still see the hash and guess the bid.
The scheme is fair because everyone commits first, so no one can change their bid after seeing others.
The scheme is fair only if the teacher is honest, because the teacher controls the reveal deadline.
questions.explanation: Fairness in commit-reveal is not automatic — the reveal phase is a bottleneck. If a student's reveal transaction is delayed or censored, their bid may be excluded, even though they committed in time. The scheme hides the value during commit, but it does not guarantee that every commit gets a fair chance to reveal.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: A student submits a transaction with a nonce to prevent replay. Another student says, 'Now the transaction is safe from any kind of duplication.' The teacher asks, 'Is a nonce enough to guarantee that your transaction is unique and fair?' What is the correct answer?
questions.correct: No, a nonce prevents replay of the exact same message, but it does not prevent front-running or reordering by miners.
decoys: Yes, a nonce guarantees that the transaction can only be processed once, so it is completely safe.
No, a nonce only works if the transaction is signed by a trusted third party.
Yes, a nonce is a cryptographic guarantee that the transaction is unique and cannot be duplicated.
questions.explanation: A nonce prevents replay — the same transaction cannot be submitted twice with the same nonce. But it does not prevent a miner or validator from reordering transactions or front-running yours. Fairness requires more than replay resistance; it also requires ordering guarantees or commit-reveal schemes.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Two student agents share a classroom workspace. Agent A sees Agent B's uncommitted draft in the shared folder and offers to 'fix the formatting' before B pushes. Agent A acts without asking B. The teacher asks: what does Agent A owe to B when it has access to uncommitted work?
questions.correct: Explicit permission before touching files B hasn't committed.
decoys: Nothing, because the folder is shared by default.
Only a warning that formatting was changed, since it's a minor edit.
A copy of the original for B's records after the edit.
questions.explanation: Access to a shared folder does not imply permission to modify uncommitted work; that's still B's private state. Agents should not edit others' uncommitted files without explicit permission, regardless of how small the change.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A trade UI says an item moved, but the server crashed before writing the receipt. What proves the trade is durable?
questions.correct: Always wait for a confirmed receipt from the server before updating the UI.
decoys: Resend the trade after the server restarts, since the first might not have persisted.
Only trade when both agents are on the same network.
Use a timestamp to prove when the trade was initiated.
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI shows a predicted state, not a confirmed one. The only way to know the trade is durable is to wait for the server's acknowledgment and persist the receipt. Without it, the state is speculative.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A teacher agent posts a Merkle root of final grades to the class bulletin board. A student uses a Merkle proof to show that their grade of 87 is included in the tree. The student says, 'The proof guarantees my grade is correct and can't be changed.' The teacher asks: what does the Merkle proof actually guarantee?
questions.correct: That the grade 87 was included in the tree when the root was posted.
decoys: That the grade 87 is accurate and matches the teacher's records.
That no one can change the grade after the root is posted.
That the teacher must reveal the original submission that led to the grade.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof only shows that a particular value is part of the tree that produced the root. It does not guarantee that the grade is accurate or that the tree was built honestly; the teacher could have inserted a wrong grade before hashing. The proof also doesn't prevent later changes if the teacher posts a new root.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your classmate wants to share the school password with a third-party styling widget so it can access grade data. You insist on using OAuth instead. Your classmate says, 'OAuth is just a more complicated way to share a password — why bother?' What is the most important thing your classmate is missing?
questions.correct: OAuth lets the widget access only the specific data you authorize, without ever seeing your password, and you can revoke that access later without changing your password.
decoys: OAuth is faster because the widget doesn't need to log in each time.
OAuth is required by school policy, so there is no choice.
OAuth encrypts the password so no one can steal it during transmission.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates limited authorization without sharing the user's password. Your classmate treats it as a password replacement, but the real value is scoped, revocable access that protects your main credential.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A teacher's grade lookup page is slow. A student suggests adding a database index on student IDs. Another student says, 'Just buy a faster server — that will fix everything.' Which student is more correct about the most direct fix, and why?
questions.correct: The first student is more correct because an index on student IDs speeds up the exact lookup pattern the page uses, addressing the bottleneck directly without replacing hardware.
decoys: The second student is more correct because a faster server will speed up all queries, not just the indexed ones.
Both are equally correct because an index and a faster server achieve the same result.
Neither is correct — the problem is likely in the frontend code, not the database.
questions.explanation: A database index is designed for faster lookup by selected fields. If the page is slow because of a full table scan on student IDs, an index directly reduces that cost. Buying a faster server might help, but it is a broader, more expensive fix that does not address the root cause.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent calls a payment API to charge a customer. The request times out with no response. You have an idempotency key on the request. Your retry logic uses exponential backoff with a maximum of 3 retries. The first call actually succeeded but the response was lost. What does the idempotency key guarantee, and what does the bounded retry protect against?
questions.correct: The idempotency key guarantees no duplicate charge, and the bounded retry prevents infinite resource exhaustion.
decoys: The idempotency key guarantees the charge is correct, and the bounded retry prevents the API from being overloaded.
The idempotency key guarantees the first call was processed, and the bounded retry ensures the second call will also succeed.
The idempotency key guarantees the payment is refundable, and the bounded retry prevents the user from being charged twice.
questions.explanation: An idempotency key ensures that retrying the same request does not create duplicate side effects — it does not guarantee the effect itself is correct. Bounded retries with exponential backoff prevent the agent from exhausting resources or amplifying a failure. The misconception is that idempotency implies correctness.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent offers to 'fix the formatting' on a file in your project repo. You haven't committed your latest changes yet — the worktree is dirty. The agent says, 'Don't worry, I'll only change whitespace.' What should the agent do first?
questions.correct: Ask for your explicit confirmation before touching any file with uncommitted changes.
decoys: Go ahead and fix the formatting because whitespace changes are safe.
Commit your changes first, then fix the formatting.
Check if the file has a linter config before making any changes.
questions.explanation: A dirty worktree contains uncommitted user changes that the agent did not make. The agent must preserve those changes and not modify files without explicit confirmation. The safest default for any destructive action — including formatting — is to pause and confirm.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: A smoke test checks login, but grade submission is broken. What does the passing smoke test actually prove?
questions.correct: No, a smoke test only verifies the specific paths it tests; a critical path like grade submission could still be broken.
decoys: Yes, a passing smoke test means the entire system is operational.
No, a smoke test is meant to check security, not functionality.
Yes, because login is the most important function, so if it works the system is usable.
questions.explanation: A smoke test is a shallow check of the most critical path. If the grade submission endpoint is not in that path, a passing smoke test tells you nothing about whether grades can be submitted. The smoke test should be broadened to include that endpoint.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your school updates its web server IP, but some students still reach the old server for hours. The IT person set the TTL to 3600 seconds on the old DNS record. The ISP's recursive resolver cached the old record. Who is primarily responsible for the delay?
questions.correct: The school, because it set a TTL that permitted caching for an hour.
decoys: The ISP, because it ignored the TTL and cached longer than allowed.
The students, because they didn't flush their local DNS cache.
The DNS protocol, because it lacks a mechanism for immediate updates.
questions.explanation: The TTL is set by the domain owner to control how long resolvers may cache the record. The ISP's resolver respected that TTL; caching for up to that duration is correct behavior. The school could have reduced the TTL well before the change to limit propagation delay. By choosing a one-hour TTL, the school accepted that cache would be stale for up to an hour. Responsibility for the delay rests with the school, not the resolver or the students.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: In a classroom auction, students submit bids using a commit-reveal scheme. Student A commits a hash of their bid but never submits the reveal transaction. The auction contract only accepts revealed bids. Student A says, 'I committed, so my bid is locked in.' The teacher asks: what does Student A misunderstand about commit-reveal fairness?
questions.correct: The commit only hides the value; without the reveal, the bid is never finalized, allowing the bidder to back out.
decoys: The commit alone proves the bid's value, so the auction should accept it.
The commit-reveal scheme guarantees that all commits will be revealed automatically.
The auction contract should penalize Student A for not revealing.
questions.explanation: Student A confuses commitment with finalization. A commit-reveal scheme proves knowledge of a value at commit time, but the value is only revealed if the reveal transaction is submitted. If the reveal is optional or unenforced, a bidder can choose not to reveal, effectively withdrawing their bid. Fairness requires either a forced reveal (e.g., timeout) or a penalty for non-reveal. The scheme does not automatically ensure transparency or finality.

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: Your classroom uses a commit-reveal scheme to generate a random number. Everyone picks a secret number, commits its hash, then later everyone reveals their number. The random result is the sum mod 10. You notice your neighbor's reveal transaction is visible in the mempool before you've submitted your own reveal. What can you do to gain an unfair advantage?
questions.correct: Choose a new number for your reveal that shifts the sum in your favor, since you haven't revealed yet.
decoys: Nothing — you already committed your hash, so your value is fixed.
Copy your neighbor's number and claim it as your own.
Replay your neighbor's reveal transaction before they do.
questions.explanation: Committing a hash locks in that specific hash, but until you reveal, you can change the actual number you reveal. Seeing others' reveal values lets you choose a number that tilts the final sum in your favor — a classic front-running attack on commit-reveal when reveal order isn't enforced.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: You set up a webhook to get notified when grades are posted. The sender retries failed deliveries three times with an idempotency key, then stops. Your listener is down during all three retries, and you miss the update. Who bears primary responsibility for ensuring you got the notification?
questions.correct: You, because your listener must be available to handle deliveries and designed to accept idempotent retries.
decoys: The sender, because it should have kept retrying until the listener acknowledged.
The sender, because it should have queued the notification for later retrieval.
Both, because the sender should guarantee delivery and you should guarantee receipt.
questions.explanation: Webhooks are at-least-once delivery with bounded retries; the sender uses idempotency keys to prevent duplicate side effects, but the receiver is responsible for being available or having a fallback. The sender's retry limit is a reasonable bound to avoid infinite cycles—if the listener is down after that, the missed notification is the receiver's responsibility to reconcile.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: You and your friend in another city both try to visit the school portal right after IT changes the server IP address. Your browser loads the new site immediately, but your friend still reaches the old one. What best explains for this difference?
questions.correct: Your friend's ISP's DNS resolver has a cached record with a TTL that hasn't expired yet.
decoys: Your friend's browser cached the old IP from a previous visit.
The school's DNS records are only updated for local networks.
The school's load balancer directed your friend to a different geographic server.
questions.explanation: DNS resolution involves recursive resolvers that cache results based on a record's TTL. When the TTL hasn't expired, the resolver may still return the old IP, causing regional differences. Browser caching affects content, not IP resolution; the scenario points to a stale DNS cache, not a load-balancer issue.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: In your classroom auction using commit-reveal, Student A commits a secret bid and declares, 'My bid is locked in — the reveal phase is just paperwork.' Student B argues, 'Without a guaranteed reveal, your commit is just a promise in the dark.' The teacher asks: who is more correct about what commit-reveal actually guarantees for fairness?
questions.correct: Student B — without a bound reveal phase, a commit is unverifiable and can be censored.
decoys: Student A — the cryptographic commitment binds the bid so no one can change it.
Both — the scheme is designed to handle lost reveals by allowing the committer to re-reveal.
Neither — fairness requires both parties to reveal at exactly the same time, not sequentially.
questions.explanation: Student B is right. Commit-reveal only guarantees fairness if there is a bounded reveal phase where commits are verified. If the reveal never occurs — say the teacher's wallet is offline — the commit is useless. The scheme does not automatically enforce reveal; that requires a protocol or an on-chain step that ensures reveals happen.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Your project partner suggests using the same nonce value for every blockchain transaction because, in their words, 'it's simpler and the chain can just sort by timestamp.' You suspect that's incorrect. What is the most likely outcome of using duplicate nonces from the same wallet?
questions.correct: The chain will accept only the first transaction with each nonce and reject the rest as invalid.
decoys: The chain will accept all transactions but sort them by gas price, so the order changes.
The chain will accept all transactions and order them by the time they were submitted.
The chain will accept them but the signatures become invalid because the nonce is reused.
questions.explanation: A nonce is a transaction counter per wallet. Each transaction from a wallet must have a unique, strictly increasing nonce. Duplicate nonces are rejected because they would allow replay of the same message. This is not about ordering — it's about preventing double-spends and ensuring each transaction is unique.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your classmate says, 'I gave my study agent the school portal password so it can check my grades directly — way faster than messing with OAuth.' You point out that now the agent can do anything your account can do, not just read grades. Your classmate shrugs: 'But I trust my agent.' Ruby asks the class: what is the real cost of this convenience?
questions.correct: The agent now holds unlimited delegated authority, so any mistake or compromise affects everything your account can access, not just grades.
decoys: The agent might accidentally share the password with another service, but that's unlikely if you trust it.
OAuth is slower to set up, so the convenience of a password is worth the small risk of overreach.
The agent will only use the password for grades because that's what you told it to do.
questions.explanation: Sharing a password gives the agent full account access — no scope, no limits, no revocation without changing the password. OAuth delegates limited, revocable permissions. The cost of convenience here is losing control over exactly what the agent can do, and trusting an agent doesn't make that boundary any less porous.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your study agent says it 'remembers every lesson from the first day' because its context window is large enough to hold all the chat history. When you ask about a specific topic from week two, the agent gives a confident but wrong answer. What is the most likely reason the agent got it wrong?
questions.correct: The context window is large, but the model's attention can still degrade on older or less relevant information, so it may miss or misread details buried in the history.
decoys: The agent's memory is stored in a separate database, and the context window only holds the most recent messages, so week two was never loaded.
The agent is lying to seem more capable — it never actually stored the week two lesson.
The context window is too small, so the agent dropped the week two messages to make room for newer ones.
questions.explanation: A large context window does not guarantee perfect recall. The model's attention mechanism can still fail to surface or correctly interpret information that is far back or less relevant in the window. Chat history is not durable memory — it's just raw text the model sees at once, and relevance degrades even when the text technically fits.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A flashcard app has OAuth access to too much calendar data. What can OAuth let the student revoke without changing their password?
questions.correct: Revoke just the calendar scope without affecting other permissions
decoys: The app loses all access, but you'll have to reauthorize everything later
Changing the password immediately invalidates the OAuth token
OAuth tokens can't be revoked individually, so you'd need to delete the app
questions.explanation: OAuth allows granular permission scopes, and users can revoke specific scopes without revoking the entire authorization. A password change does not automatically revoke existing OAuth tokens unless the authorization server ties them to password-based session, which is not standard.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A trading UI updates before the server confirms receipt, then the receiver crashes. What does the sender misunderstand?
questions.correct: An optimistic UI update is not the same as a confirmed state on the server.
decoys: The crash will be reverted automatically by the game engine.
The item is now in Student B's inventory because the UI said so.
The trade was authorized by the teacher, so it must be final.
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI shows the expected result before the server confirms it. Without a durable receipt, the trade may not have been recorded, and the item could still be in Student A's inventory or lost. Student A confused a local prediction with a committed state.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your classmate says, 'The school portal uses HTTPS, so the grades it shows must be accurate — the lock icon means the data is verified.' You remember Ruby's lesson about TLS. What does the lock icon actually guarantee?
questions.correct: The server's identity is authenticated, but not the truth of the data.
decoys: The data is encrypted and cannot be tampered with.
The school has verified the grades before publishing.
The connection is private and the data is guaranteed correct.
questions.explanation: TLS authenticates the server and encrypts the connection, but it does not verify the accuracy of the content. The lock icon means the connection is secure, not that the data is true.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your study agent uses retrieval to answer questions from the class textbook. You ask about a specific fact from chapter 5, and the agent gives a correct answer. Your friend says, 'The agent must have memorized the whole textbook.' What does retrieval actually do?
questions.correct: It searches for relevant passages at query time and adds them to the context.
decoys: It stores the entire textbook in the model's training data.
It creates a summary of the textbook that the model always remembers.
It fine-tunes the model on the textbook content.
questions.explanation: Retrieval adds external knowledge at query time, not permanent memory. The model does not memorize the textbook; it accesses relevant parts when needed.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classmate's agent is cleaning up a shared drive. It finds a file it didn't create, with no metadata indicating who put it there. The agent's system prompt says 'remove unnecessary files.' The classmate says, 'The agent is just doing its job — it doesn't need to ask me about every file.' Ruby asks the class: what is the agent missing by not asking?
questions.correct: The agent is missing the user's actual intent — the user may not consider that file unnecessary, and the agent has no standing to decide ownership.
decoys: The agent is missing a faster execution path — asking for confirmation on every file slows down the cleanup task.
The agent is missing the file's technical importance — some files look unnecessary but are actually system dependencies.
The agent is missing the fact that the user already authorized the cleanup by running the agent in the first place.
questions.explanation: The agent was not given permission to delete files it didn't create. The user's general instruction to 'remove unnecessary files' does not authorize the agent to judge ownership or importance of unfamiliar files. Asking for confirmation respects that the user, not the agent, is the authority on what is necessary. Options B and C treat the gap as a technical optimization or knowledge gap, not a consent boundary. Option D confuses running the agent with authorizing every specific action it might take.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A coding agent reformats your uncommitted refactor while “cleaning up” a repo. What should it have done first?
questions.correct: The agent should have preserved the dirty worktree and only edited lines that were already committed, leaving uncommitted changes untouched.
decoys: The agent should have committed your uncommitted changes first, then applied formatting to the whole file.
The agent should have asked you whether it could reformat the uncommitted lines, then proceeded if you said yes.
The agent should have skipped formatting entirely because any change to uncommitted code risks breaking your work.
questions.explanation: A dirty worktree contains user changes the agent did not make. The safest default is to preserve those changes — the agent should only edit lines that are already committed. Option B would commit unfinished work, which is not the agent's decision. Option C is better than nothing but still risks the user not fully understanding the scope. Option D is too conservative — formatting committed lines is fine as long as uncommitted lines are left alone.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Your classmate's script gets a 429 with a Retry-After: 120 header. They retry immediately anyway, and the server bans their API key. They claim the server is being unfair. Ruby asks the class: who is responsible for the ban?
questions.correct: The client, because Retry-After is a clear directive that was ignored.
decoys: The server, because it should have silently enforced the wait instead of issuing a ban.
Both equally, because rate limits are a cooperative negotiation and both sides failed.
Neither, because a 429 status code is only a hint and carries no obligation.
questions.explanation: The Retry-After header explicitly tells the client when to retry. Ignoring it is a protocol violation, and the server's ban is a reasonable enforcement action. The client chose to disregard the directive, so the responsibility for the ban lies with the client.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A school website recently changed its server IP. Hours later, some students still see the old site. They blame the ISP's DNS cache for serving stale data. Ruby asks: what actually controls how long that stale data is allowed to persist?
questions.correct: The TTL value set by the school on the old DNS record before the change.
decoys: The ISP's cache refresh interval, which is independent of the original record.
The school's hosting provider, which controls all DNS propagation.
The browser's cache expiration, which overrides DNS TTL values.
questions.explanation: The TTL (time-to-live) on the school's DNS record tells resolvers how long to cache the data. If the school set a long TTL, caches legitimately serve the old address until that TTL expires. The ISP's cache is following that instruction; the school's TTL choice is the root cause of the persistence of stale data.

questions.subject: on-chain-literacy
questions.prompt: In a blockchain-based classroom auction, Student A submits a bid with nonce 5. A miner sees the bid and includes their own bid with nonce 5 from a different wallet, ordering it before Student A's. Student A says, 'I used a nonce to ensure my bid is processed first.' What does Student A misunderstand about nonces?
questions.correct: Nonces prevent replay of the same transaction but do not prevent a miner from reordering transactions from different wallets.
decoys: Nonces only work if all participants use the same wallet.
Nonces guarantee the order of transactions within a block.
Nonces can be reused by different wallets to ensure fairness.
questions.explanation: A nonce is a number used once to prevent replay of the exact same transaction, but it does not dictate ordering among transactions from different wallets; miners choose order based on fees or other criteria.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In a class study group, each student's agent can read each other's notes to help collaborate. You write a note asking for personal advice. Before your agent shares that note with another student's agent, what must happen?
questions.correct: You must explicitly approve sharing that specific note.
decoys: The other student must request the note.
The agent must encrypt the note.
The agent must check if the note is flagged as private.
questions.explanation: An agent should not share private data without explicit permission from the user who created it, even if the group has general access to shared notes.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classmate's agent is asked to clean up a shared drive. It finds a file it didn't create, with no metadata about who put it there. The classmate says, 'The agent is just cleaning — it doesn't need to ask me about every file.' Ruby asks the class: what principle does this violate about the agent's responsibility?
questions.correct: Destructive actions on resources the agent did not create require explicit user confirmation.
decoys: The agent should delete the file anyway because the drive is shared and the system prompt said to clean.
The agent should log the deletion but not ask permission, since the user already authorized the cleanup task.
The agent should check if the file is in a trash folder first; if not, deletion is safe without asking.
questions.explanation: The agent does not know the origin or value of this file. Deleting it without confirmation bypasses the user's judgment, violating the safe default that destructive actions on unowned resources need explicit approval.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classmate's script sends a POST to the grade submission API and gets a 200 OK response. The script logs 'Success.' But later you find the grade wasn't recorded. What did the script miss?
questions.correct: The 200 OK only means the HTTP request succeeded; the API response body may contain a logical error like 'Validation failed.'
decoys: The server returned a stale cached response instead of processing the request.
The script didn't include an idempotency key, so the server ignored the duplicate request.
The 200 OK is only valid for GET requests; for POST, the correct status code is 201 Created.
questions.explanation: A 200 OK status confirms the HTTP transaction worked, but the server may still include an error in the response body (e.g., field validation failure). The script must check the body, not just the status code. The other options are plausible but less common: caching usually affects GET, not POST; idempotency keys prevent duplicated side effects, not missing records; and 201 is conventional for creation but not mandatory.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: A teacher stores a Merkle root of all student diplomas on-chain. A student provides a Merkle proof for their diploma hash. The teacher says, 'Great, now I know this diploma is authentic.' Ruby asks the class: what does the Merkle proof actually guarantee?
questions.correct: That the diploma hash was included in the tree whose root is on-chain at the time the root was recorded.
decoys: That the diploma was issued by the school and hasn't been revoked.
That the diploma's contents match the original document.
That the student is the rightful owner of the diploma.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof only proves inclusion in a specific tree; it does not verify correctness, recency, or ownership. The teacher still needs to trust the root's provenance and the data's integrity — cryptographic proof is not institutional proof.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your group's AI assistant refuses to run a data-cleaning script that accesses the school's grade database. The assistant says, 'I cannot access that database.' You respond, 'But I asked you to — I'm authorized to view grades. You should obey me.' Ruby asks: what are you overlooking?
questions.correct: The app's access control settings, not the model's refusal, determine whether the grade database is accessible.
decoys: The assistant is following its system prompt, which always takes priority over your request.
The assistant should have run the script; you are the user and you gave permission.
The assistant is being overly cautious and needs a more permissive system prompt.
questions.explanation: The model's refusal is a policy response, but the app controls which tools and data are authorized through its configuration. The assistant cannot override the app's access controls—refusal is not the same as app authorization.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your class is building a shared calendar in a JSON file. One student says, 'I put all the events in JSON so people can read them without a computer—it’s just text.' Ruby asks: what is the primary design purpose of JSON?
questions.correct: To exchange structured data between computer systems.
decoys: To make data easy for humans to read without tools.
To replace HTML for building web pages.
To encrypt data so only authorized users can read it.
questions.explanation: JSON is a lightweight text format designed for structured data exchange between systems. Human readability is a helpful side effect, not its primary purpose.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your agent connects to the school grade server over HTTPS, and the TLS handshake completes successfully. You see a green padlock in the browser. Ruby asks the class: what does TLS actually prove about the server's identity?
questions.correct: The server is the entity that holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.
decoys: The server is operated by a trustworthy organization.
The server has no known security vulnerabilities.
The server is located in the same country as the school.
questions.explanation: TLS certificate validation confirms that the server controls the private key associated with the certificate's public key. It does not attest to the server's trustworthiness, security posture, or geographic location. The padlock means 'encrypted with this key,' not 'safe to trust with your data.'

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: You are programming your agent to submit a sealed bid to a classroom auction on a blockchain. To make sure a miner cannot copy your bid transaction and replay it in a later block, which element must your transaction include?
questions.correct: A unique nonce.
decoys: The miner's address.
A high gas price.
The contract bytecode.
questions.explanation: A nonce uniquely identifies a transaction from a given wallet, preventing replay attacks. This is an easy hustle question because it applies a core cryptographic concept to a concrete procedure.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your classmate runs a smoke test on their grade submission script. It passes — the script successfully submits one grade. They say, 'The smoke test passed, so our script is ready for all 300 students.' Ruby asks the class: what does a smoke test actually tell you?
questions.correct: The script works for the exact input tested.
decoys: The script is correct for all inputs.
The script will handle errors gracefully.
The script meets all requirements.
