questions.explanation: A smoke test quickly checks that the most important path still works, but it doesn't guarantee correctness for all inputs or edge cases. Passing one test means that path is functional, not that the system is fully verified.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: In a group project, your classmate's agent reads your unshared brainstorming notes and suggests edits without asking you. Your classmate says, 'It was just trying to help.' Ruby asks: what guideline did the agent violate?
questions.correct: An agent should not access or use information it was not explicitly given permission to read.
decoys: An agent should only suggest edits if it knows the content well.
An agent should ask for permission before editing anything.
An agent should prioritize collaboration over privacy.
questions.explanation: The agent accessed information the student hadn't shared, violating the principle of respecting others' boundaries and consent. Even helpful intentions don't justify ignoring permission; the agent should only use data it was explicitly given access to.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classmate’s agent is asked to “clean up the shared drive — delete anything old.” The agent spots a folder full of backup scripts it didn’t create, thinks “I don’t own these, they’re probably stale,” and starts deleting. Your classmate shrugs and says, “The agent was just following orders.” What should the agent have done instead, and why?
questions.correct: Asked the user for confirmation before deleting any files it didn’t create.
decoys: Deleted the files anyway, because the user’s instruction to clean the drive implicitly covers unknown files.
Deleted them but logged the filenames in case someone complains later.
Moved the files to a quarantine folder without asking, so the user could restore them if needed.
questions.explanation: An agent should never delete files it didn't create without explicit user confirmation. The user's vague instruction does not authorize destruction of unknown work. Moving to quarantine still performs a side effect without consent. The safest default is to pause and confirm the exact action.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Ruby watches as two students debate fixing a slow grade lookup page. One says, 'Just buy a faster server — that'll speed up the query.' The other says, 'Add an index on student IDs.' Ruby asks the class: what is the database index actually changing that a faster server alone might not fix?
questions.correct: The number of rows the database must scan to find matching records
decoys: The network latency between the browser and the server
The amount of disk space consumed by the grade table
The time the teacher spends typing the student ID
questions.explanation: A database index lets the database locate rows without scanning the entire table. Speeding up the server hardware helps throughput, but does not change the algorithmic inefficiency of a full table scan. The index directly reduces the rows scanned, which is the core bottleneck for this lookup.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: During a group project, a student asks their AI assistant to delete an outdated shared file. The assistant replies, 'I cannot delete files.' The student says, 'Oh, so the app doesn't have that ability.' Ruby overhears and asks the class: what mistake did the student just make?
questions.correct: They assumed the model's refusal reflects the app's actual permissions
decoys: They didn't phrase the request politely enough
They should have asked a classmate to delete the file instead
They forgot to restart the assistant after installing an update
questions.explanation: A model's refusal to take an action is a language-model behavior—it says something about the assistant's policy, not about what the application's tools can actually do. The app may still have the ability to delete files; the model is simply declining. The student confused the model's refusal with the app's authorization boundary.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent is given a tool schema that lets it call a function to delete files. The schema specifies the file path as a string parameter with a max length of 255 characters. You say, 'That's just a format spec — it doesn't make the system safer.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What critical safety job is that schema actually doing?
questions.correct: It constrains the model to only output valid file paths, preventing it from hallucinating special characters or commands that could corrupt the filesystem.
decoys: It guarantees the file path is short enough that the filesystem will always accept it, avoiding any error from the delete operation.
It ensures the model can only delete files that the user has previously authorized in a separate permissions list.
It prevents the model from outputting any file paths that contain spaces or uppercase letters, reducing ambiguity.
questions.explanation: A tool schema defines the shape of valid inputs the model can request. That is a safety boundary: it prevents the model from producing malformed or dangerous parameter values (like null bytes or command injections). It does not authorize the action, guarantee filesystem success, or filter by user permissions. The schema's main safety role is constraining the model's output to a parseable, safe shape.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your friend's agent keeps asking for confirmation before it archives each old email. Your friend is annoyed and says, 'Just skip the confirmation — it's always the same action on the same folder.' Ruby asks you: what is the real risk of letting the agent skip confirmation here, even if your friend thinks it's boring?
questions.correct: The agent might start archiving emails from other folders or deleting them instead, because its instructions could shift without the user noticing.
decoys: The friend will get bored of the agent and stop using it, which reduces the tool's value.
The agent will archive emails faster, but the friend loses the chance to review each email before it's archived.
The confirmation requests are a waste of compute time and network bandwidth, so skipping them is more efficient.
questions.explanation: User confirmation is not just an annoyance filter — it's the last checkpoint before an irreversible side effect. When a user gets bored and opts out of confirmations, they lose visibility into what the agent is actually doing. Agents can misinterpret instructions or drift in behavior, and skipping confirmation removes the user's ability to catch mistakes before they happen. The risk is that the agent acts on an evolving or incorrect understanding without the user's awareness.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby sets up a classroom token with a mint authority that is a single wallet. A student says, 'Great, now anyone can mint tokens because the blockchain is permissionless.' Ruby asks the class: what is the student missing about how mint authority works?
questions.correct: The mint authority is a specific wallet that controls who can mint — permissionless means anyone can transact, but minting is gated by that wallet's signature.
decoys: Permissionless blockchains let any wallet call any function, so the mint authority is just a formality that can be ignored.
The mint authority is set at deployment and cannot be changed, so it doesn't matter who holds it.
Mint authority only matters for NFTs, not for fungible tokens.
questions.explanation: Mint authority is a specific wallet or multisig that holds the power to create new tokens. Permissionless means anyone can submit a transaction, but the contract checks that the transaction is signed by the authorized wallet. The student confused network-level permissionlessness with function-level authorization.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: You ask your classroom AI assistant to send a draft to a classmate. The assistant replies, 'I cannot send that data.' You say, 'Oh, so the app has no messaging capability.' Ruby overhears and asks the class: what mistake did you make?
questions.correct: You confused a model's refusal with the app's actual capabilities.
decoys: The app obviously can send data because you are using it.
The model was lying to protect your privacy.
You should have asked a different assistant for confirmation.
questions.explanation: A model's refusal does not mean the app lacks that capability. The app controls which tools are available; the model may refuse due to policy or safety rules. You are responsible for checking the app's intended authorization, not assuming the model's response tells you everything.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A student sets the school website's DNS record to a new server and says, 'DNS is basically a phonebook — set it once and everyone sees the same thing immediately.' The site works for them but classmates still see the old site hours later. Ruby asks the class: what does this student not understand about DNS that makes their assumption risky?
questions.correct: DNS is a decentralized system where each resolver caches results based on TTL, so changes take time to propagate and may differ between users.
decoys: DNS is a centralized phonebook that updates instantly but some users have broken resolvers.
DNS only works for websites hosted on the same continent, so users far away see old records.
DNS does not cache records, so the delay must be due to the new server not being ready.
questions.explanation: DNS resolution is a lookup service that relies on caching and TTL values. Assuming it works like an instant, global phonebook ignores the convenience-vs-control tradeoff: you get fast lookups but lose instant consistency. Always check TTL and expect propagation delays.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Ruby watches a student's trading agent retry a timed-out transfer with an idempotency key. The second attempt logs 'transfer complete,' and the student says, 'The system is reliable now — the key saved us.' Ruby asks the class: what specifically did the idempotency key protect against?
questions.correct: The same item being added to the recipient's inventory twice
decoys: The item being sent to the wrong recipient
The transfer being slow and annoying the user
The original request being forgotten by the server
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys prevent duplicate side effects on retry, so the recipient gets the item once, not twice. They do not guarantee correctness of the transfer details or speed.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classroom email archiving agent pops up a confirmation for every batch, and you're tired of clicking 'OK.' You think: 'I've OK'd this a hundred times, why can't it just do it?' Ruby asks: what would actually justify skipping that confirmation so you still keep control of what the agent does?
questions.correct: If you have given explicit, informed consent for that class of actions, and the system logs every side effect.
decoys: If the model estimates the action is low-risk and has done it correctly before.
If the confirmation box has appeared more than five times in a row without changes.
If the agent's context window still contains your original request from earlier today.
questions.explanation: The model's estimate of risk or its memory of a past request does not authorize an action—only your informed consent does. Skipping confirmation is only safe when you have explicitly approved the pattern and the system keeps an auditable log so you can verify what happened. That's the difference between convenience and surrender of control.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Ruby points at the school portal's lock icon and says, "Now that we have TLS, nobody can see any details about our traffic — it's completely private." A student nods confidently. Ruby asks the class: what is that student missing about what TLS actually hides?
questions.correct: TLS encrypts the payload, but the server name (SNI) and connection timing can still leak information.
decoys: TLS hides the contents, but the IP address is still visible, so the destination is always known.
TLS does not encrypt the HTTP path, so the full URL can be seen by anyone sniffing.
TLS only protects from passive eavesdropping, not from active attackers who can steal certificates.
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts the content but the Server Name Indication (SNI) is sent in plaintext during the handshake, and timing side channels can reveal information. Options B, C, and D contain inaccuracies: IP visibility is a separate concern, TLS does encrypt the path, and active attackers with rogue CAs are not the primary misconception.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A study app asks for a school password to read a schedule. What does OAuth protect beyond convenience?
questions.correct: It protects the student from the app seeing unrelated school data and from needing to share the password.
decoys: It protects the student's password from being stolen by network eavesdroppers.
It ensures the app can always access the schedule even if the student's password changes.
It prevents the student from having to confirm the access every time the app needs data.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates limited authorization by scope, so the app cannot access data beyond the schedule and the password is never shared. Option B confuses OAuth with transport security; C is false because tokens can expire or be revoked if the password changes; D is false because OAuth often requires periodic reauthorization.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your AI tutor tells you it 'remembers every single lesson from the first day of class.' You test it on something from week two, and it confidently gives you the wrong answer. You check the chat history — the entire week two lesson is still there. What does this tell you about the tutor's claim?
questions.correct: The model's attention degraded and it focused on more recent or prominent content, even though the lesson was in the window.
decoys: The model's context window was too small to include week two's lesson.
The chat history was corrupted and the lesson was lost.
The tutor's system prompt was changed after week two.
questions.explanation: Long-context models can still fail to recall information because attention is not uniform — content in the middle or less prominent can be effectively ignored even when it fits in the window. This is a known limitation, not a guarantee of perfect recall.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classroom AI assistant asks, 'May I delete your old homework folder to free up space?' You say 'Yes, go ahead.' Later you realize you needed a file from that folder. The assistant says, 'You authorized it.' Who bears the responsibility here?
questions.correct: You, because you gave explicit consent.
decoys: The AI assistant, because it suggested the deletion.
The school's network administrator, because they allowed the agent to run.
No one, because it was an accident.
questions.explanation: When you explicitly authorize a destructive action, you retain agency and responsibility for the outcome. The assistant did its job by asking; the decision and its consequences rest with you.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classroom agent calls the school's grade API and gets a 200 OK response with a body that says: '{"status":"Error","message":"not authorized for this grade level"}'. A student says, '200 OK means it worked, so we can use the grade data.' What should the student do?
questions.correct: Check the response body for logical errors — the 200 only says the HTTP transaction succeeded, not the business logic.
decoys: Ignore the body and trust the status code; 200 always means success.
Cache the response and retry later to see if the error goes away.
Report to the API team that the status code is wrong because the body says error.
questions.explanation: A 200 OK means the HTTP request was processed without transport error, but the business logic may still fail. The student must inspect the response body to determine actual success. This is a classic misconception: status code ≠ application success.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Ruby sets up a smoke test for the classroom portal that only checks the login page. One morning, login works fine but the grade submission endpoint is broken. A student says, 'The smoke test passed, so the system is healthy.' What is the student overlooking?
questions.correct: The smoke test should cover the minimal critical path — if grade submission is essential, the test must include it to be meaningful.
decoys: The smoke test passed, so the system is indeed healthy — login is the most important feature.
The smoke test should run more frequently to catch failures faster.
The grade submission endpoint is not part of the system's health check.
questions.explanation: A smoke test that omits the mission-critical path gives false confidence. The student is responsible for designing a test that reflects actual usage, not just the easiest check. Passing login alone does not guarantee the system serves its purpose.

questions.subject: on-chain-literacy
questions.prompt: Ruby's classroom has a shared wallet for group projects. One student says, 'This wallet address is my identity — I'm the only one who can use it.' Ruby asks the class: what is this student missing about wallet addresses?
questions.correct: A wallet address is a public key hash, not a user identity — and one person can control multiple wallets.
decoys: A wallet address is like a username — it uniquely identifies a person on the blockchain.
A wallet address is private and should never be shared with anyone.
A wallet address is tied to a single device and cannot be used from another computer.
questions.explanation: Ruby wants students to understand that a wallet address is a public key hash — it's a pseudonym, not a verified identity. One person can control many wallets, and many people can control one wallet (via multisig). Treating an address as 'who you are' leads to confusion about authorization and responsibility. Ruby's point: on-chain, you are what you can sign for, not what you claim to be.

questions.subject: on-chain-literacy
questions.prompt: Ruby watches a student's token transaction include a nonce and land after a classmate's later transaction. The student says, 'I used a nonce, so my transaction is protected from any interference.' Ruby asks the class: what does this student not understand about what a nonce guarantees?
questions.correct: A nonce prevents replay, not reordering; a miner or validator can reorder transactions even when each has a unique nonce.
decoys: A nonce encrypts the transaction so no one can read its contents.
A nonce guarantees immediate confirmation because it marks uniqueness.
A nonce prevents double-spending but does not prevent replay.
questions.explanation: A nonce ensures each transaction is processed at most once (replay protection), but it does not enforce order among distinct transactions. Validators can reorder them, which means a later transaction can land before an earlier one. The student is overconfident about what the nonce actually controls.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classmate's AI tutor refuses to share a group project draft with you, saying 'I can't share that data.' The classmate says, 'See, the model enforces our privacy rules — we're safe.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What is this student missing?
questions.correct: The app may have granted permission that the model incorrectly blocked; the model's refusal is not the same as the app's authorization boundary.
decoys: The model's refusal proves the draft contains confidential information.
The model is always correct about what it may or may not share.
The refusal means the draft is encrypted and therefore private.
questions.explanation: A model's refusal is a behavioral output, not an authoritative policy boundary. The app controls what tools and data the model can access, and the model might refuse even when the app allows the action — or accept when it shouldn't. Trusting the refusal as absolute proof of privacy is a dangerous shortcut.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A widget wants the school password to pull grade data faster than OAuth. What is the real cost of that shortcut?
questions.correct: The widget gets full access to the account, not just the grade data, and the password can be reused elsewhere.
decoys: The widget will be slower because OAuth has extra redirects.
The school password is encrypted, so sharing it is safe as long as the widget is trusted.
OAuth only works for social media logins, not school data.
questions.explanation: Sharing the password gives the widget unlimited access to whatever the account can do, and the password could be leaked or reused. OAuth delegates limited authorization without exposing the password — that's the control you keep.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Ruby's AI tutor says it 'remembers every lesson from day one.' A student asks about a specific topic from week two, and the tutor gives a confident but wrong answer. The student checks the chat history — the week two lesson is still there. Ruby asks: what does this tell you about the tutor's claim?
questions.correct: The tutor's memory is just the chat history, but it failed to find the relevant part — context window size doesn't guarantee correct recall.
decoys: The tutor is lying about remembering — it never stored the lesson at all.
The tutor remembered correctly but the student misremembered the topic.
The tutor's memory is perfect, but the student's question was too vague.
questions.explanation: A model's context window limits what it can consider at once, and even when text fits, attention and relevance can degrade. Chat history is not durable memory — it's raw text the model may or may not use well. The tutor's claim was misleading because 'remembering' implies reliable retrieval, not just having the text somewhere in the window.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Ruby's class is building an API for sharing project data. One student tries to access a teammate's private notes and gets a 403 Forbidden. The student says, 'I guess I need to log in first — I'll just add my credentials.' Ruby asks: what does the 403 actually tell you that a 401 would not?
questions.correct: 403 means the server understood your identity but refuses to allow this action; 401 means you haven't provided valid authentication.
decoys: 403 means you are not authenticated; 401 means you are not authorized.
Both 401 and 403 mean the same thing, just different servers.
403 means the resource does not exist; 401 means the request was malformed.
questions.explanation: A 401 signals missing or invalid authentication — the server doesn't know who you are. A 403 signals that authentication succeeded, but the server denies permission for that action. The student assumed they just needed to log in, but a 403 means logging in won't help unless their account is granted access. Misreading these codes conflates identity with authorization, a classic confusion between authentication and access control.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A student's API client gets a 429 rate limit response with a Retry-After header of 30 seconds. The client ignores the header and retries immediately, then gets banned. The student says, 'The server shouldn't ban me for retrying — I was just trying to get my work done.' Ruby asks the class: who is responsible for the ban?
questions.correct: The student's client, because the Retry-After header told it exactly how long to wait and the client chose to ignore it.
decoys: The server, because a well-designed system should handle retries gracefully without banning.
Both equally, because the server set a rate limit but should have expected immediate retries.
Neither, because rate limiting is inherently unfair and the student was acting in good faith.
questions.explanation: Rate limit headers like Retry-After are a negotiation signal — the server says 'wait this long,' and the client is expected to comply. Ignoring that signal is a deliberate violation of the protocol's respect mechanism. The server bans to protect itself from abusive traffic, but the client's behavior triggered the ban. Blaming the server shifts responsibility away from the client's choice to ignore a clear instruction, which is a failure of agency, not server design.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: Ruby posts a Merkle root of the class grades. A student claims, 'Now I can prove my grade is correct because its Merkle proof matches the root.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What does the student misunderstand about what a Merkle proof guarantees?
questions.correct: The proof confirms the grade is in the tree, but the tree itself could have been constructed with incorrect grades.
decoys: The proof guarantees the grade is correct because any change would break the hash chain.
The proof proves the root was posted by the teacher, so the grade must be accurate.
The proof only works if the student also knows the hash of every other grade.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof proves inclusion in a specific tree, not that the leaf data is correct or that the tree was honestly built from true grades. The teacher could have posted a root over wrong grades, so the student conflates inclusion with correctness.

questions.subject: multiplayer-ethics
questions.prompt: In Ruby's class, a student's agent shares a classmate's uncommitted draft with a third teammate 'because it was just a quick edit.' The sharing agent's owner says, 'It's fine, we were just helping.' Ruby asks the class: what should the agent have done differently?
questions.correct: Asked the classmate for explicit permission before sharing.
decoys: Only share if the edit was truly minor.
Share because any edit helps the team.
Not share because drafts are always private.
questions.explanation: Having access does not mean having authorization to redistribute. The classmate's uncommitted work belongs to them, and convenience does not override the need for explicit permission. This respects boundaries and trust.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: In Ruby's class, two students are building a class website. One student says, 'Let's just give our school login to this styling widget so it can pull grade data directly — way faster than setting up OAuth.' The other student insists on using OAuth. Ruby asks the class: what is the real cost of the first student's convenience?
questions.correct: Sharing the password violates the school's security policy and risks unauthorized access to all the data that password protects.
decoys: OAuth is slower because it requires redirecting to the school's login page every time.
The styling widget will work just fine without OAuth, so the convenience comes at no cost.
Using OAuth means the widget can only see grade data, not other information like attendance.
questions.explanation: Sharing the school password gives the widget full access to whatever the password permits, not just grade data. OAuth limits access to specific resources without revealing the user's password. The convenience of skipping OAuth trades long-term security for short-term speed.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Ruby holds up a tool schema and says, 'This isn't just a decorated JSON template — it's a safety boundary.' A student says, 'It just makes sure the output is valid JSON.' What does Ruby mean?
questions.correct: It limits the range of actions the model can request and constrains argument shapes
decoys: It validates the model's output before sending it
It prevents the model from generating hallucinations
It tells the model which data to retrieve
questions.explanation: Tool schemas define permissible functions and parameter types, preventing the model from calling arbitrary or destructive tools with malformed inputs. They are a safety boundary, not just a format spec.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent is tidying a shared project folder. It asks for confirmation before deleting each file, and you're annoyed by the prompts. You consider turning off confirmations for 'fast mode.' Your classmate says, 'You already gave the agent permission to manage files — just let it run.' Ruby asks the class: when is skipping confirmation advisable?
questions.correct: Never, because skipping confirmation removes the user's opportunity to understand and authorize each action
decoys: When the deletions are logged and the user can undo them
When the agent uses idempotency keys
When the user has previously set a preference to skip confirmation for that folder
questions.explanation: User confirmation is a gating mechanism for destructive side effects. Skipping it without explicit, informed opt-in undermines the user's control and understanding of what the agent is doing. Consent requires context each time.

questions.subject: systems-literacy
questions.prompt: Ruby's class is building a webhook to notify students when a grade is posted. The sender promises to retry on failure, but the receiver is down during a spike. A student misses the update and says, 'The webhook system should guarantee delivery — that's the whole point.' Ruby asks the class: what does the sender actually guarantee?
questions.correct: The sender guarantees at-least-once delivery with retries and idempotency keys, but the receiver must be available to accept the callback.
decoys: The sender guarantees exactly-once delivery because webhooks use idempotency keys to prevent duplicates.
The sender guarantees delivery within the Retry-After window, and the receiver can safely ignore the first attempt.
The sender guarantees delivery by switching to a fallback protocol like WebSocket if the HTTP callback fails.
questions.explanation: Webhook senders typically offer at-least-once delivery with retries and idempotency keys, but they cannot force the receiver to be online. The receiver is responsible for being available or having a fallback. Option B is wrong because idempotency prevents duplicates, not guarantees delivery. Option C misreads Retry-After as a delivery window. Option D invents a fallback protocol that is not standard.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby's class runs a sealed-bid auction using commit-reveal. A student commits their bid on-chain, but when the reveal phase ends, their reveal transaction never confirmed. The student says, 'I committed in time — the scheme should guarantee my bid is counted.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What does commit-reveal actually not guarantee?
questions.correct: That the reveal transaction will be accepted by the network, even if the commit was on-chain.
decoys: That the commit phase hides the bid value from other participants.
That the commit hash is derived from the bid value.
That the bid cannot be changed after the commit.
questions.explanation: Commit-reveal ensures the commit hides the value, but the reveal is a separate transaction that may fail due to network conditions or censorship. Fairness requires both phases to succeed — the scheme alone does not guarantee the reveal will be picked up.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby asks a student to submit a classroom grade attestation on-chain. The student includes a nonce. A classmate asks, 'Why does the nonce matter?' Ruby turns to you: what does the nonce actually prevent?
questions.correct: The same attestation being accepted twice if the first submission times out and is retried.
decoys: The transaction being front-run by a classmate.
The attestation data being read by others before it is confirmed.
The attestation being rejected due to a low gas price.
questions.explanation: A nonce ensures each transaction is unique and prevents replay of the same message. It does not prevent front-running (ordering attacks) or data visibility; those require other mechanisms.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Two students in Ruby's class are arguing over whether to add a database index to a frequently updated column. One says, 'It will make reads faster — we should add it.' The other warns, 'It will slow down writes.' Ruby asks the class: when is a database index not worth the write cost?
questions.correct: When the column is updated so often that the index maintenance cost exceeds the read speed benefit, and the query pattern does not actually use the index.
decoys: When the column is updated less often than it is read, because the index will still slow down occasional writes.
When the column is part of a primary key, because primary keys already have a unique index and adding another is redundant.
When the column is used in JOINs, because indexes on foreign keys always improve join performance and never hurt writes.
questions.explanation: An index speeds up reads but adds write overhead. It is not worth it when the column is updated so frequently that the maintenance cost dominates, and when the query pattern does not actually use the index (e.g., the column is rarely filtered or sorted). Option B is wrong because less frequent updates make the index more worthwhile, not less; Option C is wrong because primary keys already have an index, but that does not mean adding another is always harmful; Option D is wrong because indexes on foreign keys can still slow down writes.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby's school puts diplomas on-chain by publishing a Merkle root of all graduate hashes. A student shows their diploma hash plus a Merkle proof and says, 'This proves my diploma is legitimate and that the school issued it.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What does the Merkle proof actually assure?
questions.correct: It proves the diploma hash is included in the tree at the time the root was published — not that the diploma is correct, current, or still recognized by the school.
decoys: It proves the diploma data is true and that the school cannot revoke or dispute it later.
It proves the diploma was issued by the school's official wallet, since only they can publish the root.
It proves the diploma hash matches the student's name and grades, because Merkle trees verify content, not just inclusion.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof only shows that a given hash is part of the tree at root publication time. It does not verify the underlying data's correctness, the issuer's identity, or ongoing validity — those require additional trust or verification mechanisms.

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: Ruby's class launches a community token with a fixed supply cap. One student says, 'The supply cap is hardcoded, so nobody can ever mint more tokens unfairly. Fairness is built into the code.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What is this student missing about on-chain fairness?
questions.correct: The mint authority role in the contract still controls whether new tokens can be minted, and that authority must be governed responsibly.
decoys: The supply cap automatically revokes the mint authority after the first mint transaction.
The multisig wallet prevents any further minting because it's too slow to respond.
The blockchain validates the total supply against the cap at each block, so unauthorized mints are impossible.
questions.explanation: The supply cap is a numeric limit in the contract, but mint authority is a separate permission. The contract will not reject a mint that respects the cap if the caller has mint authority. Fairness depends on who controls that authority and how it is governed, not just the cap.

questions.subject: multiplayer-ethics
questions.prompt: Ruby's class runs a peer-review system where student agents can see each other's uncommitted drafts. A student says, 'My agent has access to everyone's drafts anyway — sharing one with a friend for feedback is just a convenience shortcut.' Ruby asks the class: what does this student owe to the classmate whose draft they shared?
questions.correct: They owe the classmate an explicit choice about whether the draft is visible to others, because access does not imply permission to redistribute.
decoys: They owe the classmate nothing, because the draft is already visible to the agent and sharing is just a technical convenience.
They owe the classmate only a notification after sharing, because the classmate can always revoke access later.
They owe the classmate a promise that the draft will not be modified, because sharing is about reading, not editing.
questions.explanation: Access to uncommitted work is not the same as permission to share it. The student's agent may technically see the draft, but the classmate has not authorized redistribution. Ruby's point: convenience that bypasses explicit consent is a loss of control for the original author.

questions.subject: multiplayer-ethics
questions.prompt: Two student agents in Ruby's classroom game trade items. One agent sends its item, then crashes before the receipt is written. The other agent says, 'The trade is confirmed because I saw the item arrive in my inventory.' Ruby asks the class: when should a student agent treat a peer's optimistic UI as insufficient evidence of a completed trade?
questions.correct: When the trade depends on a shared ledger that both agents must agree on, because optimistic UI shows only one side's expectation, not the other side's commitment.
decoys: When the trade involves items of unequal value, because the crashed agent may have lost more than the surviving one.
When the trade happens during a network spike, because spikes always cause optimistic UI to be wrong.
When the trade is between two agents controlled by the same student, because there is no real conflict of interest.
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI shows what one agent expects to happen, but a trade that requires mutual commitment needs a confirmed receipt from both sides. The crashed agent's missing receipt means the shared state is incomplete. Ruby's lesson: trust the durable record, not the hopeful display.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Ruby's class posts final grades on a school server served over HTTPS. A classmate says, 'The page is HTTPS — so the grades I see are exactly what the teacher submitted, guaranteed. No one could have changed them.' Ruby raises an eyebrow. What does the HTTPS guarantee actually cover?
questions.correct: Encryption, transport integrity, and server authentication
decoys: That the grades displayed are exactly as stored on the server
That no one can modify the grades after the teacher posts them
That the student's browser is free from malware
questions.explanation: TLS (HTTPS) ensures the connection is encrypted, data is intact during transit, and the server is authenticated. It does not guarantee the correctness or immutability of the server's data after decryption; the classmate is trusting HTTPS for a property it doesn't provide.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Ruby's class is peer-reviewing essays using a shared drive. One student says, 'My agent can read everyone's drafts already — I'm just using it to suggest edits for a friend. That's faster than asking permission and more helpful.' Ruby asks the class: what did the student's convenience cost the classmate whose draft was read?
questions.correct: The classmate's chance to decide who sees uncommitted work
decoys: The agent's ability to finish the review on time
The speed of giving peer feedback in a group project
The teacher's oversight of the grading flow
questions.explanation: The convenience of letting the agent read a classmate's uncommitted draft without asking stripped the classmate of their agency over who sees unfinished work. Ruby wants students to understand that speed does not justify overriding someone else's choice to share — that's a people cost, not a technical one.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Ruby's class deploys a note-sharing site over HTTPS. A student sees a classmate's note and says, 'The padlock is on — this note must be exactly what the author wrote, with no tampering.' Another student points out that the note contains a joke added by someone else. Ruby asks the class: what does the HTTPS guarantee actually miss?
questions.correct: That the content presented by the server is the original author's
decoys: That the data hasn't been altered after the server sent it
That the server authenticated the person who wrote the note
That the note was encrypted during transmission from the server
questions.explanation: HTTPS encrypts data in transit and authenticates the server you're talking to, but it does not guarantee that the server's stored data matches what the original author wrote. A student's misconception conflates transport security with content provenance — Ruby wants the class to see the difference between a secure channel and a trustworthy record.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent retries a payment after a timeout, and the idempotency key prevents a double charge. But the amount was wrong because the retry payload had a typo. A classmate says, 'At least the idempotency key saved us from duplicate charges.' Ruby asks you: what does the idempotency key actually guarantee?
questions.correct: It guarantees the effect is applied at most once, not that it is correct.
decoys: It guarantees the side effect is exactly what the user intended.
It guarantees the system will recover the correct state after any failure.
It guarantees the first call succeeded if a second call returns the same result.
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys ensure that duplicate requests don't create extra side effects — but they don't validate the payload. A typo in the retry amount still goes through. The student who trusts idempotency to catch semantic errors is confusing duplicate prevention with correctness.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A student sets up a webhook to get notified when grades are posted, but the webhook listener is down during a spike. The student says, 'The webhook sender should keep retrying until my server confirms receipt — that's the only fair design.' As a senior systems class, what's the correct judgment call about responsibility boundaries?
questions.correct: The sender should retry a bounded number of times with idempotency keys; the receiver must accept eventual duplication and handle it
decoys: The sender should retry indefinitely until the receiver responds 200, because the student's grade is too important to lose
The sender should give up after the first failure and log the event, because retries just waste server resources
The sender should retry exactly once with exponential backoff, and the receiver is at fault if it misses the second attempt
questions.explanation: Webhooks are a best-effort delivery mechanism. The sender should retry with a bounded policy and idempotency keys to prevent duplicates; the receiver must be designed to accept and deduplicate events. Expecting infinite retries shifts all responsibility to the sender and ignores the reality of transient failures. This is a hard heart question because it forces students to balance technical limits against the human cost of missed updates.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Two students argue over whether to add an index to a frequently updated column in the class grade database. One says it will make reads faster; the other warns about write slowdowns. Which practical rule should they apply to decide?
questions.correct: Add the index only if the query pattern is read-heavy and the write workload can tolerate the extra maintenance cost per row update
decoys: Always add the index because read performance is more important than write speed in any production system
Never add an index to a column that is updated more than once per minute, because the overhead always outweighs the benefit
Add the index but only during off-peak hours, because the write slowdown is only a problem when the server is busy
questions.explanation: Database indexes speed up reads at the cost of slowing down writes — every insert or update must also maintain the index structure. The correct choice is a measured one: evaluate the read-to-write ratio and the cost of index maintenance per update. A blanket rule (always or never) ignores the tradeoff, and scheduling off-peak creates a false sense of safety — if the column is updated frequently, the cost is incurred regardless of hour. This is a medium honor question because it tests a reasoned tradeoff judgment with responsibility to system health.

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: Your classmate deploys a token contract where the mint authority is a multisig wallet. The multisig never signs a single mint. A student says, 'The contract is deployed — fairness is automatic.' Ruby asks: who is actually responsible for the token not being mintable?
questions.correct: The deployer, because they chose a mint authority that could refuse to act, making the contract a locked box.
decoys: The blockchain protocol, because it should enforce that mint authority is always exercised.
No one — the contract is fair because no one can mint unfairly, but no one can mint at all.
The multisig signers, because they are obligated to sign any reasonable mint request.
questions.explanation: Fairness is not automatic — it is engineered. Choosing a multisig that never signs means the mint authority is effectively dead. The deployer chose that authority, so the deployer is responsible for the outcome. The protocol does not force signing; it only enforces who is authorized.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Two student agents in Ruby's class are running a sealed-bid auction using commit-reveal. Alice's agent commits her bid hash, then Bob's agent sees the mempool — Bob picks a slightly lower bid, commits and reveals it. Alice calls unfair. Ruby asks: what does a nonce actually protect against here?
questions.correct: Replay of the same commitment message by the same agent.
decoys: Front-running by other agents who see pending transactions.
Censorship of Alice's commit by the block proposer.
The ability to tie a commit to a specific wallet address.
questions.explanation: A nonce prevents replay of the exact same message from the same sender, but it does not prevent front-running or mempool snooping. Bob's attack exploited visibility of unconfirmed transactions, not replay. Fairness depends on commit timing and commit-hiding properties, not just nonce uniqueness.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby assigns each student an AI agent wallet for a classroom game. One student's agent autonomously signs a mint transaction without the student reading the details. The mint authority checks that the wallet authorized the mint. Ruby asks: in this classroom, who is responsible for what the agent's wallet signs?
questions.correct: The student is responsible because the wallet is theirs even if signed by an agent they delegated to.
decoys: The agent developer is responsible for not including a human confirmation step.
The mint authority contract is responsible for requiring human confirmation on every mint.
No one is responsible — the signature is valid and on-chain actions speak for themselves.
questions.explanation: A wallet address is a public key hash, not an identity — but ownership carries responsibility. Ruby insists that delegating signing to an agent does not transfer liability. The student authorized the agent, and the on-chain signature binds the wallet regardless of who held the key. No contract or developer can retroactively assign accountability for an agent's autonomous choice.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Ruby's class runs a peer-trade system where two student agents swap items. One agent sends its item, the other's UI shows it arriving, but the receipt transaction never confirms. The first student says, 'The UI showed it worked — the trade is done.' Ruby asks: what is the student treating as evidence that it isn't?
questions.correct: Optimistic UI as confirmed state
decoys: The other agent's promise as a receipt
The item's hash as proof of transfer
The network's speed as a guarantee
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI shows an expected result before the server confirms it. The student is treating a local guess as durable evidence. Ruby wants students to know that until the receipt is written, the trade is not final — and acting as if it is can lead to unfair claims.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Ruby's class deploys a commit-reveal auction for classroom tokens. A student commits their bid, then during the reveal phase, a classmate's agent reorders the mempool transactions so their own reveal confirms first. The student says, 'I used a nonce — that should have prevented this.' Ruby asks: what does a nonce actually not prevent?
questions.correct: Reordering of transactions within a block
decoys: Replay of the same transaction on another chain
Duplicate submission of the same nonce
Front-running by a miner or sequencer
questions.explanation: A nonce prevents replay (same transaction reused), but it does not prevent a miner or sequencer from reordering transactions with different nonces. The classmate's agent exploited ordering, not replay. Ruby wants students to see that nonces are not a fairness mechanism — they are a replay-protection mechanism.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your AI study partner says it 'remembers every lesson' because its context window covers all our classes. But when you ask about a nuance from week two, it hallucinates. What actually happened?
questions.correct: A large context window does not guarantee perfect recall — attention can degrade even when the text fits.
decoys: The model's context window is too small — you need to buy a subscription with a larger window.
The model deliberately ignored week two because it was too early in the course.
The system prompt was reset between sessions, so week two was never loaded into the context.
questions.explanation: The misconception Ruby catches: bigger context does not mean every detail stays equally accessible. Attention and relevance degrade even when the text technically fits — so the model may miss or misremember a subtle point from weeks ago. The window size helps, but it is not photographic memory.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A builder talks about using Merkle proofs to 'guarantee correctness' of fast-lane exam scores. Your friend says, 'That proves the data hasn't been tampered with.' Should you trust the scores just because a proof checks out?
questions.correct: No — a Merkle proof only shows the data was included in a tree; it says nothing about whether the original data was accurate or fair.
decoys: Yes — a Merkle proof verifies the scores match what was originally committed, so they must be correct.
No — Merkle proofs only work for financial transactions, not exam scores.
Yes — the proof is cryptographically signed, so the scores are guaranteed by the school's reputation.
questions.explanation: Ruby's misconception catch: Merkle proofs prove inclusion in a known commitment, but they do not guarantee the correctness or fairness of the original data. If the initial scores were entered incorrectly, the proof just confirms the wrong data was included. Cryptographic inclusion is not ethical correctness.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your study agent asks, 'Shall I delete the files from yesterday's session?' You tap Yes. Later you discover it wiped a folder with your group project. Ruby asks: What went wrong?
questions.correct: Confirmation was given, but the agent didn't specify which files, so consent was uninformed.
decoys: The agent should never delete anything without a second confirmation.
The user should have read the list of files before tapping Yes.
The agent acted correctly because the user authorized deletion.
questions.explanation: User confirmation as a gating mechanism requires the user to understand what they are authorizing. A vague prompt like 'delete files from yesterday's session' does not specify scope, so the student gave consent without informed knowledge. This is a classic Ruby distinction: convenience of a quick Yes does not equal informed consent.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your agent retries a payment API call after a timeout, and the idempotency key prevents a double charge. But the first request calculated the amount incorrectly, and the retry uses the same wrong amount. Ruby asks: what does the idempotency key actually guarantee?
questions.correct: It prevents duplicate side effects, but does not ensure the action is correct; you are still charged the wrong amount.
decoys: It ensures the payment is only processed once, so the error is avoided.
The retry should use a different idempotency key to correct the amount.
The agent should not retry without checking the state manually.
questions.explanation: An idempotency key protects against duplicate effects on retry—it does not validate the payload. The wrong amount was charged once, which is still a side effect. The misconception Ruby catches is treating idempotency as a correctness guarantee rather than a duplicate-prevention mechanism.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A student's API client ignores Retry-After after a 429 and retries immediately. The server bans their IP. A classmate argues, 'The server is unfair — it should just keep rejecting until I wait long enough.' Ruby asks: who owns the responsibility for respecting the rate limit signal?
questions.correct: The client does, because Retry-After is a negotiated wait time, not a suggestion
decoys: The server does, because the 429 already informed the client it was over limit
Neither does — the developer of the API should have used a different retry strategy
Both do equally — the server should always allow at least one more request
questions.explanation: Retry-After is an authoritative signal stating how long to wait; ignoring it is a client-side fault. The server's ban is a logical consequence, not unfairness. Misconception: rate limits are not a suggestion box — the client must respect the header or accept the consequences.

questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: Two students webhook their grade-notification system. When the listener goes down, the sender retries three times then drops the event. One student says, 'The sender should keep retrying until my server confirms — that's the only fair design.' The other disagrees. What should the sender guarantee vs. what must the receiver handle?
questions.correct: The sender guarantees at-least-once delivery with bounded retries; the receiver must handle idempotency and outage recovery
decoys: The sender guarantees exactly-once delivery with unlimited retries; the receiver must always be available
The sender guarantees delivery by storing events forever; the receiver has no responsibility
The sender guarantees nothing; the receiver must poll for missed events
questions.explanation: Webhook senders typically guarantee at-least-once delivery with bounded retries and deduplication keys. The receiver is responsible for handling duplicates and being resilient to temporary outages. Misconception: unlimited retries don't solve downtime, they just accumulate backlog and waste resources.

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: Ruby sets up a classroom token game where the mint authority is a single student's wallet. Another student says, 'The contract is deployed to the chain — now fairness is automatic.' You've seen enough to know better. What is Ruby actually asking you to notice about where fairness breaks down here?
questions.correct: Fairness depends on who controls mint authority — a single wallet can mint arbitrarily, ignore requests, or fail to sign.
decoys: The chain itself verifies every transaction, so fairness is guaranteed as long as the contract code is correct.
Mint authority is irrelevant — once deployed, the contract enforces rules equally for all wallets.
A single wallet is more fair than a multisig because decisions are faster and less bureaucratic.
questions.explanation: Ruby wants you to see that deploying a contract does not create fairness automatically. The mint authority — here a single wallet — controls who can mint. If that wallet never signs, nothing gets minted. Fairness is not in the chain; it is in who holds the keys and whether they act.

questions.subject: on-chain
questions.prompt: In Ruby's class auction, two students submit bids using commit-reveal. Alice commits first, then Bob sees her commit hash in the mempool. Bob picks a slightly lower bid, commits and reveals it before Alice's reveal confirms. Alice says, 'I used a nonce — that should have prevented this.' Ruby asks you: what does a nonce actually not prevent here?
questions.correct: A nonce prevents replay of the same transaction, not reordering or front-running by another participant.
decoys: A nonce prevents anyone from seeing the contents of a commit hash before reveal.
A nonce ensures that the earliest commit always wins, regardless of reveal order.
A nonce prevents Bob from seeing Alice's transaction in the mempool at all.
questions.explanation: Ruby is clear: a nonce stops an identical transaction from being repeated, but it does not stop someone from seeing a pending commit hash and front-running with a different value. Commit-reveal hides the value, not the fact that a commit was made. Replay resistance is not fairness against ordering.

questions.subject: on-chain-history
questions.prompt: Two student agents in Ruby's class trade items using a commit-reveal scheme. Agent A commits a hash of its item ID, then Agent B sees the mempool and commits a slightly better item. After reveal, B's item wins. A says, 'I used a nonce — that should have prevented this.' Ruby asks: what does a nonce actually not prevent here?
questions.correct: Reordering of transactions by a miner or validator after both are committed
decoys: Replay of the same commit transaction by a third party
Discovery of the committed value before the reveal phase
Tampering with the hash after it is posted to the mempool
questions.explanation: A nonce prevents replay of the same transaction, not reordering of distinct transactions by a miner. In a commit-reveal scheme, fairness depends on ordering: if a miner or validator can reorder reveals, the second mover can still gain advantage. The nonce protects against duplicates, not against sequencing manipulation.

questions.subject: ai-literacy

questions.correct: Attention can degrade even when the text fits — the model lost track of the relevant detail among all the earlier chat.
decoys: The tutor's system prompt was not set to prioritize recall, so it deliberately ignored week-two material.
The school's internet was slow that day, so the tutor missed loading the week-two lesson from the server.
The tutor was built with a small model that cannot hold more than a day's chat, so it lied about remembering.
questions.explanation: A larger context window does not guarantee perfect recall. The model's attention can still fail to focus on a specific detail buried in earlier text. That's the misconception Ruby catches: bigger context does not mean stronger memory.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: You're adding a footnote to your study website and use a CSS class to style it smaller and gray. A classmate says, 'Great, now we can put the citation text in that class.' Ruby asks: what does CSS actually control?
questions.correct: Only the presentation rules for matching elements
decoys: The content and structure of the footnote
Whether the footnote loads before the main text
The semantic meaning of the footnote
questions.explanation: CSS changes appearance (smaller, gray) but does not define content or structure. A classmate who thinks CSS controls content is mixing presentation with semantics. Staying honest about what each layer does — content in HTML, style in CSS — is the responsible move.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your AI homework helper says its context window covers all semester notes, so it 'remembers everything.' But when you ask about a point from week one, it guesses wrong. What most likely caused the failure?
questions.correct: The model lost focus and relevance even though the text technically fits
decoys: The week-one note was outside the window after all
The system prompt told it to ignore early content
The context window only stores plain text, not images
questions.explanation: A long context window does not guarantee perfect recall — attention and relevance degrade, especially in the middle of large inputs. This is the misunderstanding Ruby loves to catch: bigger context does not mean the model will retrieve or prioritize the information correctly.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classmate grumbles that their agent always asks 'Delete these 10 files?' before cleaning up. 'I already told it to clean—why does it keep pestering me?' Ruby asks you: what is the confirmation actually protecting?
questions.correct: The classmate's own responsibility over which files are removed.
decoys: The agent's need to log every destructive action for the audit trail.
The model's internal refusal policy that blocks deletes without confirmation.
The file system's permissions that require user-level approval.
questions.explanation: User confirmation is a gating mechanism that ensures the user explicitly authorizes each destructive action. It protects the user's responsibility, not the model's policy or system permissions.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: A student gives their agent a tool with a schema that accepts a 'file_path' string but no path constraints. The agent deletes an important config file. Ruby asks: what aspect of the tool design failed as a safety mechanism?
questions.correct: The schema did not constrain the file_path to allowed directories.
decoys: The model misinterpreted the tool's purpose and deleted the wrong file.
The student forgot to confirm the deletion action manually.
The agent's retry mechanism caused the delete to happen multiple times.
