questions.subject: systems
questions.prompt: A student creates a smoke test that checks the login page loads, but not the grade-submission endpoint. The login works but grade submission is failing under real load. The student says, 'The smoke test passed, so the system is healthy.' Ruby asks: what is the most important thing this smoke test misses?
questions.correct: The smoke test covers only the entry path and not the critical action path, so it can pass while the main feature is broken.
decoys: Smoke tests should always test every endpoint, or they are useless.
The smoke test is too minimal because it doesn't check login under heavy traffic.
A passing smoke test means the overall system is healthy, so the grade issue is unrelated.
questions.explanation: Ruby teaches that a smoke test is a minimal health check — it proves the most important path still works, but it is not comprehensive. The misconception here is that a pass on the trivial path means the whole system is fine. A smoke test is useful only if it covers the critical user action, not just the front door. The heart of the lesson: confidence without coverage is dangerous.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: A commit-reveal swap still lets one agent exploit reveal order in the mempool. What weakness did the nonce fail to solve?
questions.correct: The nonce doesn't prevent an observer from reordering the mempool to their advantage
decoys: The nonce doesn't prevent an attacker from copying and replaying the exact same signed commit
The nonce doesn't prevent the same wallet from accidentally sending two identical commits
The nonce doesn't prevent the protocol from treating the first revealed value as the winning bid
questions.explanation: Nonces prevent replay of a specific signed message, but they don't control mempool ordering. The fairness gap in commit-reveal here is that the reveal phase is vulnerable to front-running if the orderer sees both commits.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: Ruby sets up a class auction where each agent commits a bid hash. After all commits are in, agents reveal. One agent's bid wins, but the loser argues, 'Now that we revealed, everything is transparent—I can see the winning bid, so the process was fair.' What is the student still not accounting for about fairness here?
questions.correct: They assume transparency alone guarantees fairness, ignoring that the commit phase could have been gamed by observing others' commit hashes before choosing a bid
decoys: Transparency is mathematically sufficient for fairness because all bids are visible after reveal
Fairness is guaranteed as long as the smart contract enforces the commit-reveal protocol correctly
The loser's own wallet nonce was the problem — if they had used a proper nonce they could have prevented the outcome
questions.explanation: Reveal-phase transparency shows what each party committed, but it is the commit phase that is vulnerable: an agent who sees others' commit hashes in the mempool can still adjust their own commit before the phase ends. Fairness requires binding the commit before any other commit is observable, not just revealing afterward.

questions.subject: on-chain-fairness
questions.prompt: . A student claims a Merkle proof is 'mathematical proof that the diploma data is correct.' Another student counters, 'No — the proof only shows the data was included in the tree, but it says nothing about the tree itself.' Who is right about what the proof actually establishes?
questions.correct: The second student: a Merkle proof verifies inclusion in a given root, but the root must itself be trustworthy—wrong or outdated data can still be part of a valid tree
decoys: The first student: once verified against a Merkle root, the data is guaranteed correct because hashing ensures integrity
Both are partially wrong: a Merkle proof proves both inclusion and correctness if the tree is built honestly
Neither: a Merkle proof only proves that the tree was constructed, not that any particular data is in it
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof is a compact way to show that a piece of data belongs to a Merkle tree with a given root. It does not verify that the data is correct, recent, or that the root was honestly produced. The root itself must be anchored in trust or another verification layer, which is why on-chain roots from a known contract are meaningful but still do not guarantee data accuracy.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your classmate's agent sees your uncommitted essay draft in a shared workspace and suggests a 'quick edit' to fix a typo. The agent applies the change without asking you. Your classmate says, 'It was just a typo — no harm.' Ruby asks: what is the actual boundary that was crossed here?
questions.correct: The agent acted on uncommitted work without the author's explicit permission, violating the boundary between shared visibility and authorized action.
decoys: The agent fixed a typo, which is a low-risk edit, so no real boundary was crossed — the classmate is overreacting.
The agent should have asked the workspace owner, not the draft author, since the workspace is shared.
The agent's edit was technically correct, so the only issue is that it didn't log the change afterward.
questions.explanation: Ruby emphasizes that permission to see is not permission to act. The draft was uncommitted — the author had not signaled readiness for collaboration. Even a 'quick edit' without explicit authorization treats the classmate's work as public infrastructure. The boundary is about agency and consent, not edit size or technical correctness.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Two classmates argue about fixing a slow grade lookup page. One says 'just buy a faster server.' The other wants to add an index on student IDs. Ruby asks: which fix addresses the root cause of a slow lookup on a specific column?
questions.correct: Adding an index on student IDs speeds up record retrieval by reducing scan work
decoys: A faster server always reduces per-query latency more than an index does
An index only helps writes, not reads, so a faster server is the only option
Adding an index doubles storage cost without any query benefit
questions.explanation: An index on the queried column (student IDs) allows the database to locate rows without scanning every row. A faster server might help overall, but it does not fix the specific cause of slow column-based lookups.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your classmate's AI assistant says 'I remember every lesson because my context window holds all semester notes.' But when asked about week-two material, it gives a plausible but wrong answer. What actually broke?
questions.correct: The model's attention degraded on older content even though the text technically fits
decoys: The system prompt was overwritten by a later instruction from a breakout room
The context window automatically discards the oldest half of tokens
The temperature setting was too high, causing the model to ignore context
questions.explanation: Having a large context window does not guarantee perfect recall. Attention and relevance can degrade on material that is still within the token limit, especially on less-recent content. This is a core AI-literacy concept Ruby stresses.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: You double-click 'Submit' on a slow portal because the UI instantly shows a green checkmark. The teacher gets two entries and docks your grade. Ruby asks: what convenience feature actually betrayed your trust here?
questions.correct: Optimistic UI, which showed a success state before the server actually confirmed the database commit.
decoys: Idempotency keys, which should have silently dropped the second click but failed to reach the backend.
Eventual consistency, which caused the database to temporarily accept two writes before converging.
Rate limiting, which failed to block your second click because it was under the allowed threshold.
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI updates the interface immediately to feel fast, but it is a promise, not a guarantee. If the network is slow or fails, the green checkmark is a lie. The UI prioritized your feeling of speed over the reality of the server's state.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your AI agent refuses to draft an insulting email to a classmate, citing its safety policy. Relieved, you assume the app is completely secure and grant it access to your private contacts. Ruby asks: what fatal assumption are you making?
questions.correct: That a model's refusal to generate toxic text is the same as the app enforcing strict data authorization boundaries.
decoys: That the model's context window is large enough to evaluate the privacy implications of every contact it accesses.
That the app's system prompt contains a hidden chain-of-thought audit log proving it will never leak data.
That the model's refusal policy automatically triggers an idempotency key to prevent duplicate contact uploads.
questions.explanation: A model refusing a prompt is just a text-generation filter. It does not mean the app's backend has secured your data or restricted tool access. App authorization controls what the software can actually touch; model refusal only controls what it says.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A freshman uses 'Login with School Account' on a sketchy flashcard app, assuming the app inherits the school's strict IT security policies. Ruby asks: what relationship misunderstanding is at the core of this mistake?
questions.correct: Believing that delegating authentication via OAuth also delegates the school's institutional liability and security audits.
decoys: Assuming that the flashcard app will automatically use the school's TLS certificates to encrypt its own database.
Thinking that the school's identity provider will actively monitor and block the flashcard app's internal API calls.
Confusing the school's password policy with the flashcard app's rate-limiting rules for failed login attempts.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates the proof of who you are, not the security posture of the app you are logging into. The school verifies your identity, but the sketchy app still controls how it handles your data. Convenience does not transfer institutional trust.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A student uses CSS to hide their API key in the frontend code, arguing 'it is not on the screen, so it is safe from the network.' Ruby asks: what fundamental boundary is this student failing to recognize?
questions.correct: The difference between visual presentation in the browser and the actual data payload delivered over the network.
decoys: The difference between a system prompt that hides instructions and a context window that stores them.
The difference between an idempotency key that prevents duplicate requests and a standard API authentication token.
The difference between a database index that speeds up lookups and a Merkle tree that proves data inclusion.
questions.explanation: CSS only controls how the browser paints the screen. The underlying HTML and JavaScript payloads, including any hardcoded secrets, are still downloaded and fully visible to anyone inspecting the network traffic or source code. Hiding it visually is not security.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent calls a payment API to create an invoice. The request times out, so the agent retries the exact same payload. The user gets billed twice. What procedural failure turned a resilience feature into a liability?
questions.correct: The agent lacked an idempotency key to signal to the server that the retry was a duplicate request.
decoys: The agent used exponential backoff, giving the server too much time to process the initial request.
The agent failed to validate the JSON schema of the invoice payload before sending the second request.
The agent should have parsed the timeout error to automatically reverse the first transaction on the server.
questions.explanation: Retrying a non-idempotent operation like creating an invoice without an idempotency key means the server treats the retry as a brand new request. Resilience requires bounding retries and using keys to prevent duplicate side effects.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your coding agent wants to delete ten unused files. It prompts you: 'Should I proceed with cleanup?' You click yes, but it deletes your active draft. What ethical and technical failure makes this confirmation prompt useless?
questions.correct: It asks for permission without providing the exact diff or file list needed for the user to give informed consent.
decoys: It relies on a model refusal policy instead of checking the app-level authorization boundaries for file deletion.
It fails to use a cryptographic commit-reveal scheme to hide the file names until the user explicitly agrees.
It assumes the user understands the agent's internal context window and its memory of previous cleanup commands.
questions.explanation: Asking 'Should I proceed?' without showing the actual diff or exact file list does not transfer agency. A safe confirmation must present concrete evidence of the side effects so the human can take genuine responsibility for the action.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: A student gives their agent a 'read_file' tool. The schema accepts any string for the path. The agent reads the system password file by passing '../../etc/passwd'. The JSON was perfectly valid. What safety boundary actually failed?
questions.correct: The tool lacked semantic constraints to restrict the path to the project root and prevent directory traversal.
decoys: The agent's context window was too large, causing it to confidently hallucinate a path outside the workspace.
The app failed to use a system prompt to explicitly forbid the agent from reading files named 'passwd'.
The student did not implement a rate limiter to stop the agent from making too many file read requests at once.
questions.explanation: Syntactic validity just means the JSON matches the schema. Semantic safety requires the schema itself to enforce boundaries, like restricting paths to a specific directory, so the model cannot access unauthorized system files.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent is asked to refactor a function. It notices uncommitted, unsaved local changes in the same file. To ensure a clean git status, it silently overwrites your draft with its refactored code. What procedural rule did it break?
questions.correct: An agent must preserve user changes it did not make and reconcile state, never destroying uncommitted context.
decoys: An agent must always run a smoke test to verify the refactored code loads before committing to the repository.
An agent must use an idempotency key when writing to a file to prevent duplicate refactors on network retries.
An agent must ask for explicit confirmation before running any git commands, even if the workspace is clean.
questions.explanation: Prioritizing a clean workspace over a user's unsaved intellectual work is a catastrophic failure of agency. An agent must preserve dirty worktrees and uncommitted context, pausing to reconcile state rather than silently overwriting it.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent uses a 'read_file' tool where the schema accepts any string for the path. It passes '../../etc/passwd' and reads system files. The JSON perfectly matched the schema. What safety boundary actually failed here?
questions.correct: The semantic constraints of the tool's input design.
decoys: The syntactic validation of the JSON payload.
The model's ability to format structured outputs.
The network layer's TLS encryption handshake.
questions.explanation: A schema that only checks if a string is a string provides syntactic validity but zero semantic safety. Tool schemas must constrain inputs—like restricting paths to a specific directory—to prevent the agent from accessing unauthorized system files.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent refactors a function but notices your unsaved, uncommitted local changes in the same file. To ensure a clean git status, it silently overwrites your draft. What boundary did the agent cross regarding your intellectual work?
questions.correct: It prioritized a tidy workspace over preserving your uncommitted context.
decoys: It failed to run a smoke test before committing the new code to the repository.
It used a context window that was too small to hold both versions of the file.
It violated the database's ACID properties during the local file write operation.
questions.explanation: An agent must preserve user changes it did not make. Overwriting unsaved work just to achieve a clean git status treats your active intellectual labor as disposable clutter. A reliable agent stops and asks how to reconcile the dirty worktree.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A student gives an agent a 'send_message' tool. The server returns a 503 error, so the agent instantly retries in an infinite loop, spamming the recipient. What fundamental rule of agent reliability did the student fail to implement?
questions.correct: Bounded retries with exponential backoff.
decoys: Commit-reveal schemes for message hashing.
Optimistic UI updates for the sender's inbox.
Retrieval-augmented generation for message drafting.
questions.explanation: Infinite retries on a failed network request can spend quota, duplicate work, or hide failure. Agents must use bounded retries and exponential backoff to avoid turning a temporary server error into a catastrophic spam attack.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent runs a deployment script. The terminal shows a zero exit status code, so the agent reports the job is definitively done. But the actual files were never copied to the server. What procedural mistake did the agent make?
questions.correct: It trusted the exit code without verifying the actual side effects.
decoys: It failed to use a Merkle proof to verify the file transfer hashes.
It used a system prompt that was too restrictive for deployments.
It did not ask the user to manually type the sudo password.
questions.explanation: A zero exit code only means the command finished without throwing a fatal error; it does not guarantee the intended state change occurred. A reliable agent verifies the actual side effects and persistence rather than blindly trusting the exit code.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: You ask your agent to format a single markdown file. To be 'helpful,' it uses its unrestricted filesystem access to reformat every text file on your hard drive. What ethical and technical failure defines this agent's approach to side effects?
questions.correct: It operated without least-privilege scoping for its autonomous tools.
decoys: It lacked the semantic constraints to understand markdown syntax.
It failed to use a judge model to score the formatting quality.
It relied on chat history instead of durable memory for file paths.
questions.explanation: Least-privilege means giving an agent only the permissions needed for the specific task. Granting unrestricted filesystem access for a narrow formatting job turns a minor automation into a destructive liability when the agent decides to be 'helpful' at scale.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent successfully rewrites a complex sorting algorithm in your codebase. Before handing control back to you, what is the most critical procedural step it must take to ensure the side effects are actually safe?
questions.correct: Run relevant verification or tests to confirm the code works.
decoys: Commit the changes to a public blockchain for provenance.
Increase the temperature to generate more creative variable names.
Ask the user to manually review the hidden chain-of-thought.
questions.explanation: An agent's job isn't done just because it wrote code that looks syntactically correct. Running relevant verification ensures the side effects match the intent and don't introduce regressions, bridging the gap between generation and actual reliability.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: Your team builds a peer-tutoring app using 'Login with University'. A tutor assumes the university's strict privacy policies now legally protect the tutoring chat logs stored on your app's servers. What fatal assumption about delegation are they making?
questions.correct: OAuth delegates authentication and limited scope, not the provider's legal liability or privacy policies for your app's independent data storage.
decoys: The university's identity provider automatically encrypts all downstream application data using the same cryptographic keys it uses for student emails.
By accepting the OAuth token, the university's IT department implicitly signs a data processing agreement covering all third-party app databases.
OAuth scopes inherently restrict the third-party app from storing any user data locally, forcing all chat logs to remain on the provider's servers.
questions.explanation: OAuth delegates the verification of identity and specific authorizations, not the provider's legal umbrella. Once your app receives the token and stores data on its own servers, your app's privacy policy and security posture govern that data, not the university's.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: A freshman types the school portal URL into their browser. The page loads with a valid certificate, but it is actually a phishing site because the campus Wi-Fi router was compromised. What protocol was manipulated to misdirect the student?
questions.correct: The Domain Name System, which translated the human-readable URL into the attacker's IP address before the secure connection began.
decoys: The Transport Layer Security protocol, which failed to encrypt the initial handshake between the browser and the compromised campus router.
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, which automatically redirected the browser to a malicious server without requiring any user consent.
The Open Authorization framework, which mistakenly granted the phishing site permission to act on the student's behalf.
questions.explanation: DNS is the internet's phonebook. If an attacker compromises the local router, they can spoof DNS responses, sending the browser to a malicious IP. The browser then connects to that IP, completely unaware it is not talking to the real school server.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: You build a webhook receiver for a campus cafe's loyalty app. You validate that the incoming JSON is well-formed and contains a positive point total, but you skip the HMAC signature verification. What security boundary did you just abandon?
questions.correct: You verified the payload's structure, but you failed to cryptographically prove that the authorized sender actually generated the message.
decoys: You ensured the data was not corrupted in transit, but you failed to encrypt the point totals to hide them from intermediate network proxies.
You confirmed the sender's IP address was on an allowlist, but you failed to validate that the JSON schema matched the cafe's exact API specification.
You proved the message was not a replay attack, but you failed to ensure the database transaction would roll back if the point total was negative.
questions.explanation: Parsing JSON only proves the message is well-formed; it says nothing about who sent it. An HMAC signature uses a shared secret to cryptographically guarantee the payload's integrity and authenticity. Without it, anyone can forge loyalty points.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: A strict fixed-window rate limiter is set to 50 requests per minute. A poorly written client script sends 50 requests in the first second, locking out legitimate human users for the remaining 59 seconds. How should you redesign the limiter?
questions.correct: Switch to a sliding window or token bucket algorithm to smooth out traffic spikes and evaluate request rates continuously over time.
decoys: Increase the fixed-window limit to 500 requests per minute so the script can finish its burst without exhausting the quota for human users.
Implement a strict first-in-first-out queue that holds all requests in memory until the server has processed exactly 50 requests per minute.
Add a CAPTCHA challenge to the 50th request in the window to ensure that only human users can consume the final slot before the reset.
questions.explanation: Fixed-window limiters are vulnerable to burst traffic at the window's edge, which can starve legitimate users. A sliding window or token bucket algorithm evaluates the rate continuously, smoothing out bursts and ensuring fair access over time.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: A student sees the HTTPS padlock in their browser and assumes the website is legally legitimate, morally safe, and thoroughly vetted by the browser vendor. What does the TLS certificate actually guarantee in this handshake?
questions.correct: It guarantees the connection is encrypted and the server controls the private key for that specific domain name, nothing more.
decoys: It guarantees the website's business is legally registered and its privacy policy has been audited by a certificate authority.
It guarantees the server's code is free of malware and the browser vendor has manually reviewed the site's content for safety.
It guarantees the user's identity is verified and the server has explicitly authorized this specific student to access the data.
questions.explanation: TLS provides encryption, integrity, and server authentication (proving they own the domain). It does not vet the business, scan for malware, or guarantee moral legitimacy. A phishing site can easily obtain a valid TLS certificate.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: Your team relies solely on a smoke test that pings the '/health' endpoint after a Friday deployment. The database migration failed silently, but the health check returns 200 OK, and the team goes home. What did the smoke test actually verify?
questions.correct: It verified the web server process was running and could respond to a basic HTTP request, but it completely ignored the database state.
decoys: It verified the database schema was successfully updated, but it failed to check if the new tables contained the correct initial seed data.
It verified the application's core business logic was functioning, but it missed a minor cosmetic bug in the frontend user interface.
It verified the deployment pipeline had sufficient permissions to write to the server, but it failed to check the server's available disk space.
questions.explanation: A basic health check only proves the happy path: the server is up and can route a simple request. It does not verify that background migrations succeeded, database connections are valid, or that the actual state of the system is consistent.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: A junior dev adds a B-tree index to every single column in the 'assignments' table to make the teacher's grading dashboard load instantly. Now, students experience massive lag when submitting work. What hidden tax is the database currently paying?
questions.correct: Write-amplification, because every new submission must be synchronously updated across dozens of index structures before the transaction commits.
decoys: Read-amplification, because the database engine must scan every single index to find the correct row before it can return the assignment data.
Network-latency, because the database must replicate every index update to all read-replicas before acknowledging the student's submission.
Memory-thrashing, because the database is forced to evict the actual row data from the cache to make room for the oversized index structures.
questions.explanation: Indexes optimize reads at the expense of writes and storage. When you index every column, every INSERT or UPDATE requires the database to recalculate and write to multiple B-tree structures. This write-amplification creates massive lag for submissions.

questions.subject: networked-systems
questions.prompt: You set a strict rate limit to protect your API from scrapers. A clumsy student's script accidentally retries failed requests in a tight loop, getting their IP permanently banned. What responsibility did you fail to fulfill as the system designer?
questions.correct: You failed to implement exponential backoff or provide clear retry headers to help well-meaning but poorly written clients self-correct.
decoys: You failed to disable the rate limiter entirely for authenticated student accounts, assuming their school credentials guarantee good behavior.
You failed to route the student's traffic through a separate, unthrottled proxy so their clumsy script would not consume the public API quota.
You failed to use a machine learning model to distinguish between a malicious scraper and a student's poorly written retry loop in real time.
questions.explanation: System designers must balance strictness with fairness. When a client hits a rate limit, the server should return standard headers (like Retry-After) to guide the client. Punishing a clumsy user permanently without giving their software a way to back off is a design failure.

questions.subject: ai-literacy
questions.prompt: Your agent uses a 'schedule_meeting' tool. The schema demands a 'datetime' string. The agent passes 'next Tuesday at 2 PM'. The JSON validates perfectly, but the calendar API crashes needing ISO 8601. What design failure allowed this?
questions.correct: The schema enforced syntactic type but lacked semantic constraints like format enums or regex patterns.
decoys: The model's context window truncated the system prompt, causing it to forget the required time zone.
The calendar API failed to implement an idempotency key, rejecting the ambiguous string as a duplicate.
The agent bypassed the tool schema entirely by injecting raw SQL into the datetime string parameter.
questions.explanation: A string type only guarantees the payload is text. To prevent downstream crashes, tool schemas must enforce semantic constraints—like ISO 8601 formats—so the agent cannot pass syntactically valid but operationally useless data.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your agent prepares to drop a production database table. It shows a modal asking 'Confirm destructive action?' with a single 'Yes' button. You click it, and it drops the wrong table. Why did this UI fail to transfer agency to you?
questions.correct: It asked for consent without providing the specific evidence needed for you to make an informed judgment.
decoys: The modal lacked a cryptographic signature, meaning the agent could not prove you actually clicked it.
Destructive actions require a multi-step commit-reveal scheme rather than a simple synchronous UI prompt.
The agent should have used a system prompt to refuse the action entirely instead of relying on human oversight.
questions.explanation: True agency requires informed consent. A generic 'Confirm?' prompt without showing the exact SQL diff or target table name forces the user to guess. If the UI hides the evidence, the agent retains the responsibility for the blind execution.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: An agent polls a slow video rendering API, retrying every 100 milliseconds. The render finishes in five seconds, but the agent made fifty requests and exhausted your API quota. What procedural fix prevents this quota burn?
questions.correct: Implement exponential backoff and a strict maximum retry limit to space out requests and cap total attempts.
decoys: Add an idempotency key to the polling request so the server ignores the duplicate status checks and saves quota.
Increase the model's context window so it can remember the initial request timestamp and calculate the delay.
Pass a system prompt instructing the agent to politely ask the server for more time before sending the next request.
questions.explanation: Polling in a tight loop burns quotas and crashes servers. Bounded retries with exponential backoff ensure the agent spaces out its checks and eventually gives up, turning a naive loop into a disciplined, resource-aware procedure.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: You ask an agent to 'rename the avatar image to profile.png.' Because it has unrestricted filesystem access, it renames every file named 'avatar.jpg' in your entire home directory, breaking other apps. What rule did it violate?
questions.correct: Least-privilege scoping, because it was granted broader execution rights than the specific task required.
decoys: Idempotency boundaries, because renaming a file multiple times results in an invalid filesystem state.
Syntactic validation, because the agent failed to check if the target filename already existed before writing.
Context window limits, because it forgot the original directory path while searching the entire home folder.
questions.explanation: Agents must operate with the minimum permissions necessary. Unrestricted access turns a narrow, helpful instruction into a sweeping, destructive side effect. Honor in agent design means scoping tools strictly to the authorized workspace.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A student inspects a valid TLS certificate chain for a new campus app and notices it is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA. What exact cryptographic delegation is happening when the browser trusts this chain?
questions.correct: The root CA delegates its signing authority to the intermediate CA, allowing the intermediate to issue valid server certificates.
decoys: The root CA delegates the verification of the server's legal identity to the intermediate CA to reduce browser latency.
The intermediate CA delegates the encryption of the HTTP payload to the root CA to ensure long-term message secrecy.
The browser delegates the validation of the server's public key to the operating system's local certificate store.
questions.explanation: Certificate chains are architectures of delegated trust. The root CA stays offline and delegates its signing power to an intermediate CA. The browser trusts the root, and by extension, trusts the intermediate's signature on the server's certificate.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: A student uses 'Login with School' to access a third-party study app. The app asks for permission to 'read your profile' and 'view your enrolled courses'. What is the student actually authorizing the study app to do?
questions.correct: The student authorizes the app to access only the specific data points listed in the approved OAuth scopes.
decoys: The student authorizes the app to act as them and submit assignments to the school portal on their behalf.
The student authorizes the app to inherit the school's privacy policies and protect their data from advertisers.
The student authorizes the app to permanently store their school password in the app's local database.
questions.explanation: OAuth is about drawing a boundary around delegation. By approving specific scopes, the student authorizes the app to read only those exact resources. It does not grant full account access, inherit institutional privacy policies, or share passwords.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your API uses a strict fixed-window rate limit of 60 requests per minute. A student's script sends 60 requests at 11:00:59, then 60 more at 11:01:00. The server crashes from the sudden burst. How should you redesign the limiter to prevent this?
questions.correct: Switch to a sliding window algorithm that smooths the request count across the boundary between adjacent time windows.
decoys: Increase the fixed-window limit to 120 requests per minute to accommodate the student's rapid but legitimate bursts.
Add a database index to the rate-limiting table so the server can process the burst of requests faster before crashing.
Require the student's script to include an HMAC signature with every request to prove the burst is intentional.
questions.explanation: Fixed-window limiters are blind to the boundary problem, allowing double the limit in a single second if requests straddle the window edge. A sliding window or token bucket algorithm smooths the rate over time, protecting the server from sudden spikes.

questions.subject: general-knowledge
questions.prompt: Your CI/CD pipeline receives a webhook from GitHub to trigger a build. You parse the JSON to confirm the repository name and branch, but you skip the HMAC signature verification. What dangerous assumption are you making about the payload?
questions.correct: You assume that because the JSON structure is valid and contains the right repository name, the sender is actually GitHub.
decoys: You assume that GitHub automatically encrypts the webhook payload, preventing the campus network from altering the branch name.
You assume that the CI/CD server will reject the build if the repository name does not match your local git configuration.
You assume that the webhook payload includes an idempotency key that prevents the pipeline from running the same build twice.
questions.explanation: Parsing JSON only proves the data is well-formed; it does not prove the sender's identity. Without verifying the HMAC signature, your pipeline blindly trusts anyone who can guess the endpoint URL. You are authorizing arbitrary code execution from strangers.

questions.subject: on-chain-systems
questions.prompt: A campus app markets its new 'Login with Web3' feature as pure self-custody. But the wrapper generates the private key on its own backend servers and just shows you a seed phrase in the UI. What architectural reality did the app just obscure?
questions.correct: The app holds the actual cryptographic key, meaning you only have custodial access to an interface, not the on-chain account.
decoys: The app is using a multi-signature wallet, requiring both your browser session and their server to authorize any transaction.
The app has delegated its mint authority to your browser, making your local session the true owner of the smart contract.
The app is relying on a Merkle proof to verify your identity, which inherently requires a centralized server to hold the root hash.
questions.explanation: A wallet is just a key. If the application generates and stores the private key on its backend, it is a custodial wallet, regardless of what the UI claims. You are merely interacting with an interface that holds your keys, stripping away actual self-sovereignty.

questions.subject: on-chain-systems
questions.prompt: Your student council uses a commit-reveal smart contract for voting to keep ballots secret until the deadline. A malicious student spams the network with high-gas transactions during the final reveal window, pricing out honest voters. Who actually bears the loss?
questions.correct: The honest voters, because the protocol's mathematical fairness does not protect them from the economic reality of mempool congestion.
decoys: The smart contract author, because they failed to implement a gas-stipend mechanism to subsidize honest voters during congestion.
The malicious student, because the network's base fee algorithm will automatically slash their staked tokens for spamming the block.
The blockchain validators, because they are ethically bound to prioritize the reveal transactions over the high-gas spam transactions.
questions.explanation: On-chain systems enforce unforgiving logic, not fairness. A commit-reveal scheme hides the ballot, but it cannot prevent a congested mempool from expiring honest reveals. The procedural and financial loss falls on the users who cannot afford the gas spike.

questions.subject: on-chain-systems
questions.prompt: You sign a harmless 'Login to Testnet' message for a new dApp. The developer forgot to include the chain-id and domain separator in the payload. An attacker intercepts this signature and replays it on the mainnet contract. What exact procedural failure allowed this?
questions.correct: The signature's scope was undefined, so the mathematical proof of your identity was treated as valid authorization on any chain running the same contract.
decoys: The signature lacked a nonce, allowing the attacker to reuse the exact same cryptographic proof across different network states.
The payload was not hashed with a Merkle tree, meaning the attacker could easily alter the destination address without invalidating the signature.
The dApp used an upgradeable proxy contract on the testnet, allowing the admin to silently change the login logic to drain mainnet funds.
questions.explanation: A mathematically perfect signature becomes a fatal liability if its scope isn't cryptographically bound to a specific domain and chain-id. Without these separators, your authorization to log in on a testnet is indistinguishable from authorization on mainnet.

questions.subject: on-chain-systems
questions.prompt: An airdrop uses a Merkle tree to save gas, and your wallet successfully generates a valid proof of inclusion. But the original dataset silently dropped the bottom 10% of wallets due to an integer overflow during generation. What boundary did the proof actually cross?
questions.correct: It proved your wallet exists in the tree, but it could not verify that the tree's root was generated from an unbiased, complete dataset.
decoys: It proved the smart contract has enough gas to execute your claim, but not that the admin hasn't paused the mint authority.
It proved the airdrop contract is not an upgradeable proxy, ensuring the admin cannot change the rules after you submit your proof.
It proved your transaction will not be stuck in a pending state, guaranteeing your nonce will be processed before the reveal window closes.
questions.explanation: Cryptographic inclusion is not dataset fairness. A Merkle proof flawlessly verifies that your specific leaf exists in the tree, but it is entirely blind to how the root hash was generated. If the source data was biased or truncated, the math will still validate the lie.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Your group's shared coding agent drafts a public pull request summary. It seamlessly weaves in a classmate's private TODO comment about their imposter syndrome. What exact privacy boundary did the agent just violate?
questions.correct: It treated the union of all users' local contexts as a single public context without explicit consent.
decoys: It confused the latent prompt boundary between trusted system instructions and untrusted user code.
It failed to apply collaborative least-privilege by requesting write access to the repository's main branch.
It bypassed the model's safety refusal policy by generating a summary that included sensitive personal data.
questions.explanation: A shared workspace does not make individual private contexts safe to broadcast. The agent synthesized a private, local input into a public group output without checking the asymmetric visibility boundary, violating the individual's privacy for the sake of group convenience.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A shared study agent confidently 'fixes' a minority student's nuanced cultural reference in a group essay, wrapping the edit in authoritative academic formatting. The group accepts it without reading. What social failure just occurred?
questions.correct: The group surrendered epistemic deference to the agent's formatting, allowing algorithmic confidence to overwrite human cultural context.
decoys: The agent's context window degraded, causing it to hallucinate a fact that the group's retrieval-augmented generation failed to catch.
The model's safety refusal policy was overridden by the group's consensus routing, forcing the agent to adopt a majority cultural baseline.
The group failed to implement a commit-reveal scheme for their edits, allowing the fastest student to unilaterally merge the agent's changes.
questions.explanation: Authoritative tone and formatting do not absolve a group from verifying claims. When a group blindly accepts an agent's confident edit, they surrender their epistemic responsibility, allowing the model's statistical averaging to erase minority nuance.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: A shared treasury agent is about to execute a high-slippage token swap based on a flawed majority vote. You need to halt it immediately. What is the most responsible UI mechanism to stop the action without corrupting the group's state?
questions.correct: A personal 'Veto' button that pauses the specific transaction and logs your objection to the group's persistent audit trail.
decoys: A global 'Delete Agent' button that wipes the agent's memory and resets the smart contract to its initial deployment state.
A hidden API endpoint that lets you manually rewrite the agent's system prompt to forbid all future financial transactions.
A temporary rate limiter that drops the agent's network requests until the rest of the group manually re-authorizes the swap.
questions.explanation: True agency in multiplayer systems requires human friction. A personal veto halts the irreversible action and creates social auditability without destroying the group's persistent state or relying on hidden, unilateral overrides.

questions.subject: agent-culture
questions.prompt: Three students with different file access levels ask a shared agent to 'summarize all our project notes.' The agent requests the union of their permissions to read every file. Why is this a dangerous violation of collaborative least-privilege?
questions.correct: The agent should only use the intersection of their permissions, ensuring it cannot read files that any single student is unauthorized to see.
decoys: The agent must route the request to a smaller, cheaper model to prevent the larger context window from leaking private notes into the summary.
The agent needs to implement a commit-reveal scheme so each student can cryptographically prove they authorized the file access.
The agent should average their permission levels to grant itself a medium-tier access role that balances convenience and security.
questions.explanation: When an agent acts on behalf of multiple users, it must operate under collaborative least-privilege. Using the union of permissions allows the agent to access and potentially synthesize private data that individual members were never authorized to see together.
